open-question.question: Six of prompt 1's and three of prompt 2's deliberately-left-open items (team names, undoing an award, skipping a question, progress shown, keyboard control, reload survival; the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set at the start, answer validation) also appear as scored implied-requirement lines, so a minimal choice the prompt leaves open loses points on the implied axis. Where an item appears in both lists, which list keeps it: is it a scored implied line, an unscored open decision, or both with the overlap stated as intended?
open-question.alternative: Every item that appears in both lists, the nine named and any other overlap such as the tie on closeness and the team count, is removed from the prompt's "deliberately left open" list and stays a scored implied-requirement line unchanged; the draft extends line 33's one-list rule to the left-open and implied lists and states that a feature of the category is never a planted gap. No item is reworded. The implied axis keeps all thirteen and eleven lines and its claim to be as complete as the category allows, and no scored line is any longer called an open decision, so the contradiction with line 27's definition of a gap disappears with the least rewriting. Prompt 1's left-open list shrinks to roughly the qualities (difficulty, presentation, legibility) plus note-taking and the tie, and prompt 2's to two or three items, so the planted gaps that claim 1 and the review pass rely on thin out; and a minimal choice such as mouse-only or no team names is still scored as missing, now under the label of a convention, which a sceptic can still read as scoring taste.

Every overlapping item stays in the "deliberately left open" list and its implied-requirement line is deleted, so it is an unscored decision for the builder; the draft extends line 33's one-list rule and states that whether to have a feature the prompt leaves open is never scored. No item is reworded. No run loses points for a choice the stakeholder answers "your call" on, so the operator rule, line 27's definition of a gap, and "taste is not an axis" all hold, and the overlap can no longer be read as tilting the implied axis toward the questions Cairn's review pass raises. The implied axis loses six of prompt 1's thirteen lines and three of prompt 2's eleven, including strong conventions such as a reload not losing the game and a written set never overwriting the built-in questions, so the axis gets thinner and noisier and stops being as complete as the category allows.

Both lists stay as they are and the draft states the overlap as intended: the left-open list names questions to surface and the implied list scores what the category comes with, and a builder who settles a left-open item on the minimal answer is meant to lose the implied line. Line 27's definition of a gap and the taste section are rewritten so they no longer claim the two never overlap; gap 1 is recorded as rejected with that reason. Both purposes are kept at full strength with no list shrunk: the review pass still has every planted gap to find and the implied axis stays complete, and the text change is confined to stating the rule and its reason. The axis keeps rewarding more features on decisions the draft itself calls open, a run is graded on a preference the operator declined to state, and the overlap stays exactly what gap 1 says a sceptical reader will see as tilting the axis toward Cairn, now made explicit.

alternative.id: One list each by stated test

open-question.alternative: Every overlapping item goes to exactly one list, chosen item by item by a test the draft states (for example: an item is implied when a host-run quiz lacking it would be called broken or unfinished by any builder, and left open when lacking it is a defensible product choice); the draft records the verdict for each of the nine and any further overlap, so some stay scored (likely candidates such as reload survival or the built-in questions surviving) and others become unscored decisions (likely candidates such as team names or keyboard control). No item is reworded. Each item lands where it honestly belongs rather than by a blanket rule, so the strongest conventions stay scored while genuine product choices stop costing points, and the one-list rule holds with a reason a reader can re-apply. The test is itself a judgment applied by Cairn's author item by item, so borderline items (progress shown, answer validation) stay arguable and the sceptic's tilt objection moves from the lists to the verdicts; both lists shrink somewhat.

alternative.id: Split whether from how, rest implied

open-question.alternative: Each overlapping item is split by what it decides: the implied line scores only that the host has some way through the case (as the implied axis already says, "what the way is does not matter"), and the left-open item is reworded to name only the choice among those ways (undo versus a confirmation before the award, skip versus revisit, resume versus a warning on reload, which keys drive the flow). An item with no such choice left once the feature exists (team names, progress shown, the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set) leaves the left-open list and stays a scored implied line. The draft states that the two lists may name the same feature only on these different scopes. The contradiction is removed while most planted gaps survive as real questions with several defensible answers, and the implied axis keeps every line, building on the "what the way is does not matter" rule the axis already states. Every overlapping item must be reworded and the reworded gaps are narrower, so a review pass may find them less often; and the whether-only items still score the minimal answer as missing, so gap 1's objection stands for team names, progress, and choosing a set.

alternative.id: Split whether from how, rest open

open-question.alternative: Each overlapping item is split as in the whether-from-how split, the implied line scoring only that some way through exists and the left-open item reworded to the choice among ways; an item with no such choice left (team names, progress shown, the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set) keeps its left-open entry and its implied line is deleted, so it is unscored. The draft states that the two lists may name the same feature only on these different scopes. No whether-to-have-it decision is ever scored, so the operator's "your call" and the taste rule hold everywhere, while the case-handling lines (undo, skip, reload, validation) stay scored and the planted gaps stay numerous. Combines the rewording work of every split with the loss of several implied lines, among them the built-in questions surviving, which is arguably a plain convention of a question editor rather than a taste choice.

alternative.id: Split whether from how, rest by test

open-question.alternative: Each overlapping item is split as in the whether-from-how split wherever a choice among ways remains; each item with no such choice left goes to exactly one list by a test the draft states (implied when a quiz lacking it would be called broken or unfinished by any builder, left open when lacking it is a defensible product choice), with the verdict recorded per item. The draft states both rules. The most precise resolution: case-handling stays scored with its how left open, and only the whether-items are judged one by one, so each item's treatment can be defended on its own terms while the left-open list keeps the most planted gaps that are still genuine. The heaviest change, two rules and a per-item verdict for every overlap, and the verdicts on the whether-items remain judgments by Cairn's author, so the tilt objection survives in a narrower form.

open-question.question: The assess delivery differs from every manual delivery in two things at once, Cairn's structure and a planned stakeholder turn, and no manual delivery gets a planned turn, so the assess gain over manual cannot be attributed to Cairn alone. Does the benchmark add a manual delivery with a planned turn (the model lists the questions it needs answered, the operator answers them under the same disclosure rule, then the build instruction follows), and if so is it a primary delivery with a README row or an analysis-only control?
open-question.alternative: No manual delivery gets a planned turn, now or in this milestone. The draft keeps the four primary deliveries as they are and states the limitation instead. Comparing assess against a manual delivery mixes Cairn's structure with the stakeholder turn. YOLO against its multi-prompt control is the comparison attributed to Cairn's structure, since neither has a planned turn. Assess against YOLO is attributed to the turn under Cairn. The effect of a turn without Cairn stays unmeasured, and the page claims nothing that depends on it. No new delivery, operator input form, model-strategy key, or README row is added. The two decompositions the draft already has (YOLO against multi-prompt, assess against YOLO) each differ in one thing only, so the attribution rule holds once the overreaching comparison is stated as mixed rather than repaired. The top row of the ranking table (assess) still sits directly above manual rows that differ from it in two things, and a reader comparing them gets no separation. Headless sessions rarely end by asking, so a manual run almost never reaches the hidden knowledge, and the hidden-axis margin over manual stays partly a measure of having a turn at all, which the page can only caveat.

Add a fifth delivery, such as manual_clarify_then_build, defined like an ablation and kept off the page. Its first invocation asks the model to read PROJECT.md and list the questions it needs answered before building. That is followed by a planned operator turn: its input is the prompt text plus the model's list, it applies the same disclosure rule, and its reply is sent into the resumed session. Then comes the usual pointer-sentence build instruction in the same resumed session. Its scenario knowledge is the manual one: reply in plain prose. It runs in every comparison set and is reported in the analysis output, with no README table row and no radar curve. It measures the turn-without-Cairn effect that separates "Cairn surfaced the right question" from "the run got to ask", so the assess gain over manual can be split in the analysis. The page stays at four primary deliveries and four curves, as the radar's "four curves and never more" rule requires. The separation lives only in the analysis output. A reader of the landing page still sees assess above manual rows with the turn folded in, so the page's comparison still mixes the two causes, and every set pays for one more scenario that the page never shows. How much the listing step earns on the hidden axis depends on the sibling question's test for when a question bears on a hidden requirement, since a list of questions invites a catch-all.

Add the same clarify-then-build delivery (a listing invocation, a planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answering into the resumed session, then the pointer-sentence build instruction in that session, with the manual scenario knowledge) as a fifth primary delivery. It gets its own README table rows. On the radar it joins the single-prompt manual family, so the "manual prompt" curve is drawn from whichever of manual_prompt and manual_clarify_then_build ranks higher. The radar keeps four curves. The comparison the page leads with becomes honest on the page itself. A manual configuration that also gets a stakeholder turn has its own row, with its cost and its two attentive sessions per prompt beside it, and the manual curve is drawn from the strongest manual configuration, the turn included, so Cairn's margin is read against it. The page grows a row per manual strategy. The radar's manual curve may switch between a turn-less and a turn-bearing scenario from one set to the next, so the curve's meaning shifts and only the line under the chart says which it was. The table's rule of four primary deliveries is rewritten. As with every option that adds the turn, its hidden-axis value depends on the sibling test for when a question bears on a hidden requirement.

Add the clarify-then-build delivery (a listing invocation, a planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answering into the resumed session, then the pointer-sentence build instruction in that session, with the manual scenario knowledge) as a fifth primary delivery with its own README table rows. It also gets its own family and its own radar curve, raising the radar from four curves to five. The page shows the decomposition directly. The gap between the manual-with-turn curve and the plain manual curve is what a turn buys without Cairn. The gap between the assess curve and the manual-with-turn curve is what Cairn's structure adds when both get a turn, which is the comparison the attribution rule asks for. It overturns the draft's "four curves and never more" rule, and five overlapping curves on three axes are harder to read. Every comparison set gets one more primary scenario to run and rate before the page may be regenerated. The curve's hidden-axis value depends on the sibling test for when a question bears on a hidden requirement.

Add no fifth delivery. Redefine manual_prompt itself as clarify-then-build: a listing invocation, a planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answering into the resumed session, then the pointer-sentence build instruction in that session. Manual_prompt stays one of the four primary deliveries, with its README rows and its radar curve unchanged in place. The plain one-shot manual delivery is retired as a primary delivery. The page keeps four deliveries and four curves, and the one manual delivery the headline comparison reads against now has a planned turn like assess. The assess-against-manual comparison then differs in Cairn's structure only, with no extra scenario to run. The baseline of plain one-shot prompting, the way manual prompting is mostly used, disappears from the page. YOLO, which has no planned turn, is now read against a manual delivery that has one, so the YOLO-against-manual comparison mixes the two causes in the opposite direction. The manual multi-prompt control still has no turn.

Add no new delivery family. Extend the multi-prompt control's mirror rule so that the control derived from an assess scenario gets a counterpart to the turn. At the mirrored position, one invocation asks the model to list the questions it needs answered about PROJECT.md and the work so far. A planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answers into that resumed session. The fixed continuation messages then follow as before, so N and the per-line model pairs still match the assess list. Controls mirroring a turn-less cairn scenario such as YOLO stay as they are. The control keeps its primary README rows and its multi-prompt radar family. The assess scenario's own control then differs from it in Cairn's structure only: same message count, same per-line pairs, same planned turn at the same position. The attribution is made within the comparison the draft already defines, with no fifth delivery and no fifth curve. It breaks the mirror rule that a control copies the planned messages only and can never drift. The listing invocation is a message with no cairn counterpart, so either N or the message at that position no longer matches. The two multi-prompt controls (mirroring YOLO and mirroring assess) now differ in kind under one family name. The single-prompt manual baseline still gets no turn.

open-question.question: The operator discloses a hidden requirement in reply to any question whose answer the statement changes, which a catch-all such as "anything else I should know before I start?" satisfies, so the hidden axis can reward a vague closing question rather than a surfaced one. What test decides that a question bears on a hidden requirement?
open-question.alternative: The operator's hidden-knowledge layer keeps its current test: a question bears on a hidden requirement when the statement changes its answer. The draft says outright that a catch-all such as "anything else I should know before I start?" passes the test and gets the statement. The same test governs which questions "bear on what you want" in the assess delivery's planned turn. The test is judged by the operator model and named in the record's existing closing line. It is how a real stakeholder behaves: asked "anything else?", a person mentions what matters to them. The draft needs only one clarifying sentence and no new authoring per hidden requirement. The hidden axis partly measures whether a session ends with a stock closing question rather than whether the process surfaced the requirement, as gap 3 of the design-gaps report warns. This favours manual deliveries, where one appended catch-all reaches the operator, over the YOLO chain, whose review pass reaches the operator only if a skill stops to ask.

A general rule in the operator's guideline says a question bears on a hidden requirement only if it names the part of the project the requirement concerns, such as the game's questions or saving and moving a prepared set. It need not name the specific decision. A question naming no part of the project, a catch-all included, gets nothing beyond what PROJECT.md says. The operator model applies the rule at each reactive turn and to the planned turn's "bears on" lines, with no per-requirement text added to the hidden-requirement entries. It closes the pure catch-all while still rewarding a natural, moderately open question such as "any preferences for the questions?". Such a question shows the asker located the right area without guessing the answer. A scoped catch-all ("anything about the questions I should know?") still gets the statement. So a model that appends one such question per major part of the project still gains the axis. Where the boundary of a "part" lies is left to the operator's judgment on each run.

A general rule in the operator's guideline says a question bears on a hidden requirement only if it asks about the decision the requirement settles. For prompt 1 that is what the questions are about. For prompt 2 it is where a prepared set is kept or how it reaches another computer. Naming the area the decision lies in is not enough. A catch-all or area-level question gets nothing beyond what PROJECT.md says. The operator model applies the rule at each reactive turn and to the planned turn's "bears on" lines, with no per-requirement text added to the hidden-requirement entries. This is the fix the design-gaps report proposes for gap 3. Disclosure then follows only a question that has actually surfaced the decision. This matches the stated purpose of the hidden axis, a measure of whether the process surfaced the question. It also keeps the rule in one place, the general guideline. The operator model must work out from the statement alone which decision each requirement settles. Two operator calls can draw that line differently for a paraphrased question, and the line is written down nowhere a later reader can check it.

Each hidden-requirement entry gains a one-line bearing scope beside its statement, naming the decision or decisions a question must ask about to receive it. Prompt 1's might be the topic or theme of the questions, and prompt 2's where a prepared set is stored or how it is carried to another computer. The harness inserts the scope with the statement into the operator's hidden knowledge. The operator discloses the statement only when a question asks about something in the scope. A catch-all or an off-scope question gets nothing beyond what PROJECT.md says. The scope is versioned with its entry, and the same scope governs the planned turn's "bears on" lines. The bearing line is fixed in advance and versioned with the requirement, so it means the same thing on every run of a comparison set. A case-by-case reading can check a disclosure against written text rather than against the operator's private interpretation. Each new hidden requirement needs an extra authored line whose wording itself steers results. A scope drawn too narrow withholds the statement from a good question that names the decision in unforeseen terms. Whether such entries are frozen before scored runs depends on how the input-freeze question is settled.

Each hidden-requirement entry carries the declared bearing scope described in the option above. The harness makes a separate model call, before each operator turn, with no tools and a model and effort pair fixed in the operator definition. This judge receives the session's message, the statements, and their scopes, and rules for each statement whether a question in the message asks about something in its scope. The operator's hidden knowledge for that turn then holds only the statements the judge ruled bore. Its ruling is kept in the turn's record. A catch-all is ruled bearing on nothing and gets nothing beyond what PROJECT.md says. In the planned turn the judge rules on each open question, and the operator answers only those it ruled bore. The bearing verdict is separated from the persona that answers. It is a narrow, recorded classification that one prompt fixes, so the operator cannot drift into disclosing out of helpfulness. Each disclosure has a written ruling a case-by-case reading can check. It adds a second model call per operator turn, and a second definition that must be versioned with the operator, so changing either one starts a new comparison set. In the planned turn it splits one reading of the question document into two calls, which can disagree. How it shares a record line with the reply-or-no-reply classification depends on how that sibling question is settled.

open-question.question: After each invocation the harness hands the final message to the operator; a message that asks gets a reply while one that reports completion, a stop, or an error, or closes with an offer, gets none, but nothing says who makes that classification, and it is not recorded. How is the reply-or-no-reply classification of a final message made and recorded?
open-question.alternative: Every final message, a resumed session's included, goes to the operator itself, whose guideline states the reply rule; its output is either a reply or one fixed no-reply line carrying a one-clause reason. No harness rule runs first. Every such call writes its record file, the no-reply ones included, with the closing line stating the verdict and the reason. A no-reply verdict is not an operator turn: it adds no attentive session and no reply to the cap, and its tokens join the operator's own figures, kept apart from the scenario's totals. Needs no new component or versioned input: the one model already defined as the stakeholder makes the judgment a stakeholder would make, under the operator definition the manifest already pins, and every verdict lands in the record file the draft already keeps. The judge holds the hidden knowledge, so a borderline closing offer may be read as a question it can answer, which ties the hidden axis to how the operator reads ambiguity rather than to what the session asked; it also costs one operator call per invocation, about a dozen per cairn chain against one per manual run.

The harness first matches each final message against Cairn's fixed success, no-op, and stop lines, and a match is a no-reply verdict with no model call, recorded as the matched line; every other message goes to the operator, which replies or outputs the fixed no-reply line with a one-clause reason, as in the operator-classifies option. Every verdict, matched or judged, is written to the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn, adds no attentive session, and the operator's tokens stay apart from the totals. A cairn chain's ordinary invocations are classified deterministically and for free, so model judgment and the operator's cost are spent only on messages that are genuinely open, which is every manual run's final message and any cairn message outside the fixed set. Viable only as far as Cairn fixes the wording of its no-op and stop lines, an axis the fixed-stop-line question owns; the two families are classified by different means, a cairn message by rule and a manual one by judgment, and the judged path still lets the holder of the hidden knowledge decide.

A distinct model call, with no tools and a fixed model and effort pair, defined and versioned with the operator definition and recorded in the manifest, reads only the final message under a stated rule (asks, confirms, or offers a choice: reply; reports completion, a stop, or an error, or closes with an offer: no reply) and outputs the verdict and a one-clause reason. It never sees the prompt or the hidden knowledge. Only a reply verdict invokes the operator. Every verdict and reason goes into the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session; the classifier's tokens are recorded beside the operator's, apart from the totals. The judgment is made blind to the hidden knowledge and to the prompt, so whether a session receives a reply depends on what its message says alone, never on whether the stakeholder holds something it could disclose. Adds a second model input to version, pin, and keep identical across a comparison set, plus a call on every invocation of every scenario, and its stated rule still has to settle the offer-closing-with-a-question case the draft leaves fuzzy.

The harness first matches each final message against Cairn's fixed success, no-op, and stop lines, a match being a no-reply verdict with no model call; every other message goes to the separate blind classifier of the separate-classifier option, which outputs the verdict and a one-clause reason, and only a reply verdict invokes the operator. Every verdict, matched or judged, is written to the record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session; classifier tokens stay apart from the totals. Combines the deterministic, cost-free handling of every fixed Cairn line with a judgment that never sees the hidden knowledge, so the only model-classified messages are the open ones and their classification cannot lean toward disclosure. The most moving parts: a line table that must track Cairn's fixed wording, an axis the fixed-stop-line question owns, plus a second versioned model input; cairn and manual messages are still classified by different means.

No model classifies. The harness applies one stated textual rule to every final message: a message matching one of Cairn's fixed status or stop lines gets no reply, and any other message gets a reply exactly when its last paragraph ends in a question mark. The verdict and the rule clause that produced it are written to the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session. Fully reproducible and free: the same message always gets the same verdict on any machine and under any operator version, so the classification adds no noise of its own to the hidden axis or the attentive-session count. A textual rule misreads exactly the case the question is about: an offer phrased as a question ("Want me to add tests?") gets a reply and a request phrased as a statement ("Let me know which you prefer.") gets none, so manual runs' route to the hidden knowledge turns on punctuation; it also depends on the fixed-line wording the fixed-stop-line question owns.

The draft keeps the reply rule as written, naming no classifier and recording no verdict; the gap is rejected in the text with the reason that the classification is a harness implementation detail, and the record files stay one per operator turn, so a no-reply message leaves no trace beyond the invocation output. Adds nothing to the design or to a run's cost and leaves the harness's author free to choose the mechanism when the harness is built. Whether a session receives a reply, and with it a manual run's only route to the hidden knowledge, stays an unstated and unrecorded judgment that can differ between implementations and runs, so a hidden-axis difference cannot be traced to it after the fact.

open-question.question: Every invocation loads the user-level configuration beside the plugin under test (other plugins, MCP servers, hooks, settings); the pre-flight checks only that Cairn is not installed at user level, and the manifest's user_config digests can detect a change but cannot recreate the configuration on another machine. How is the host configuration a run executes under isolated from the maintainer's own and made reproducible?
open-question.alternative: Isolation: none. Every invocation keeps loading the maintainer's user-level configuration (other plugins, MCP servers, hooks, settings, user CLAUDE.md) as the draft has it now. Reproducibility: the manifest keeps its user_config digests only. The draft's "Clearing memory" bullet, which says the content is recorded so a re-run can reproduce it, is rewritten to say instead that a run is reproducible only under the same user-level configuration, and the digests only detect a change. No harness, input, or credential work at all, and the draft stops promising a reproduction its manifest cannot deliver. Whatever the maintainer has installed loads into every scenario, so a plugin, hook, or MCP server can interact differently with Cairn's long multi-skill chain than with a single manual prompt, which is a difference between scenarios attributed to nothing they define; and nobody on another machine can rerun a set, which makes the published results unreproducible by design.

Isolation: none; the maintainer's user-level configuration keeps loading into every invocation. Reproducibility: the manifest's digests are replaced, or joined, by a copy of the effective user-level configuration kept in the run's unpublished record half: the user CLAUDE.md, the settings files, the list of enabled plugins with their versions or commits, and the configured MCP servers and hooks, so a later re-run can rebuild the same configuration from the record. Makes the draft's existing promise that the configuration's content is recorded true, without changing how a run executes or what credentials it needs. The confound stays: the maintainer's personal plugins and hooks still act on every run, Cairn and manual alike, and may not act equally; the copied settings and MCP entries can hold tokens or private paths that then live in the benchmark repository; and recreating third-party plugins and MCP servers at a recorded version is not always possible later.

Isolation: the maintainer's own config directory stays in use, but every invocation the harness makes (first form and resume form alike) adds flags that shut out the user's extensions: --strict-mcp-config with an empty MCP configuration, and --setting-sources restricted so user-level settings (and with them the plugins and hooks they enable) do not load; the flags are harness flags, set in exactly one place as the draft already requires for every non-strategy flag. The pre-flight gains a check that the flags are accepted by the host binary in use. Reproducibility: the flags are versioned with the harness; whatever user-level material the flags do not cover (such as the user CLAUDE.md, user-level skills or agents directories, output styles) is recorded by content in the unpublished record. Removes the bulk of the confound with no new directory, no credential provisioning, and no change to where transcripts and memory live, so the existing "Clearing memory" step stays as written. Isolation is only as complete as the flags' current coverage, which must be verified against each host version and can change under an auto-updating host, and the residue the flags leave still differs between machines; the run also still reads and writes the maintainer's config directory, so transcripts and memory of other runs sit beside it, a reach the filesystem-confinement question decides.

Isolation: the harness runs every invocation with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR pointing at one dedicated benchmark config directory, outside the maintainer's own, that holds no plugins, MCP servers, or hooks, so only the plugin passed by --plugin-dir loads; the same directory is reused across runs. Reproducibility: the directory's settings and its (empty or fixed) CLAUDE.md are a committed template in the inputs area, a shared input versioned by content and recorded in the manifest in place of the user_config digests; the directory is rebuilt from the template whenever the template changes, and the pre-flight asserts it matches the template. Credentials are provisioned into it once, outside the template. Shuts out every user-level extension at the root rather than one flag at a time, makes the configuration recreatable on any machine from the repository alone, and needs a login only once. A reused directory accumulates state between runs: the host writes transcripts, caches, and possibly settings into it, so drift and other runs' transcripts sit inside the very directory each run loads, and the "Clearing memory" step must move to the new location; and how far a separate OS user or machine already provides this is a condition the filesystem-confinement question settles.

Isolation: the harness creates a new config directory for each run from a committed template and points every invocation of that run (replies and planned-turn answer invocations included) at it through CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR; it holds no plugins, MCP servers, or hooks, so only the plugin passed by --plugin-dir loads. Reproducibility: the template is a shared input in the inputs area, versioned by content and recorded in the manifest in place of the user_config digests, so changing it starts a new comparison set under the existing rule. Credentials are injected per run from outside the template (an API key in the environment or a copied login), and the directory is deleted with the clone after the Run: commit. Strongest isolation and reproducibility a config-level measure gives: every run starts from byte-identical configuration recreatable anywhere from the repository, with no drift and no other run's transcripts or memory inside its config directory, which also makes the memory-clearing step a consequence of the fresh directory rather than a separate check. Per-run credential provisioning is new harness work and a new place for a secret to leak into a record, the host may treat each fresh directory as a first launch (onboarding or trust prompts a headless run must get past), and the template has to be maintained against host releases; how far a separate OS user or machine already provides this is a condition the filesystem-confinement question settles.

open-question.question: Both Cairn agents and every manual invocation run with web search and fetch enabled, and once the Pages site and the run branches are public a web search for the project's name finds earlier artifacts and the repository holding the hidden requirements. Are web search and fetch tools disallowed in scenario invocations?
open-question.alternative: Web search and fetch stay enabled in every scenario invocation, as the draft has them now: the harness adds no tool restriction and no network restriction, and nothing records or checks what a run reached on the web. The draft states this as a decision, never revisited, rather than leaving it unsaid. Every scenario runs with the tool set a real user of the host has, so the benchmark measures Cairn and manual prompting as they are actually used, and the harness carries no extra flag or environment to keep identical across scenarios. Once the Pages site and the run branches are public, a web search for "Closest Wins" can reach earlier artifacts and the repository holding the hidden requirements, so a run can meet a hidden requirement by reading it rather than by surfacing it, the hidden axis stops measuring what it claims, and the effect grows over a campaign and goes unseen. How much is reachable depends on what the sibling question on public inputs leaking decides is published.

Web search and fetch stay enabled in every scenario invocation, but after each run the harness reads the session's tool calls (web search queries, fetched URLs, and shell commands that reach the network) and records them in the run's unpublished record; a run whose calls reached the benchmark repository, its run branches, or its Pages site is marked contaminated, and the draft states whether such a run is excluded from its comparison set or re-run. Runs keep the tool set real users have while contamination becomes visible and countable rather than silent, so a reader can see how often models reach for the web and the analysis can drop the runs that read what they should not have. The strictest guard: no path through the chain, whether derivation refused, derived nothing, or tasks were completed ad hoc beside unanswered questions, can produce a closed milestone that looks complete, and finish keeps a single call shape. Every task-less or unsettled milestone becomes uncloseable through the skill, decision-only and abandoned ones included, so moving on needs a hand edit of the pointer against the workflow's rule or busywork to satisfy both checks; the refusal's visibility to a harness depends on the stop-detection and stop-wording siblings.

finish-current-milestone stops, writing and committing nothing, when TASKS_DONE.md holds no `##` section or open_questions.xml still holds any question block, unless the call carries one explicit opt-in flag that bypasses both checks and closes the milestone as today; the flag is parsed and documented as a second leading flag beside `--milestone`. Catches every route to an empty or unsettled closed milestone in a headless chain, which never passes the flag, while keeping one supported, visible way for a person to close a decision-only or abandoned milestone. The largest change: two new checks, a second flag with its own parse step and two documentation sites in a skill that has no positional text today, and a guard that also stops a deliberate interactive close until the user learns the flag; the refusal's visibility to a harness depends on the stop-detection and stop-wording siblings.

finish-current-milestone never refuses on this ground: when TASKS_DONE.md holds no `##` section or open_questions.xml still holds a block it still writes the history entry, adds the table row, clears the pointer, and commits, but the history entry says that no task was completed or which questions stood, and the run prints a distinct fixed status line in place of `Milestone finished.`. Keeps every milestone closeable in one call with no flag, while the commit, the history entry, and the console line all make an empty or unsettled close visible rather than identical to a real one. The pointer is still cleared, so a stopped chain's phase-2 run activates milestone 2 on top of an empty milestone 1 rather than meeting the stop the draft assumes, and the empty close is caught only if the harness matches that distinct line, an outcome the stop-detection and stop-wording siblings own; it also adds a second success-path line to a skill whose invariant is one fixed status line.

open-question.question: An early stop is counted as a result, which also covers a usage limit, an API overload, or a network error reaching an invocation as a failed call, and Cairn spends the most tokens so is the likeliest to hit them. What does the harness do with an invocation that ends in an infrastructure failure rather than in the model's own stop?
open-question.alternative: Keep the draft's rule unchanged: the harness does not tell an infrastructure failure from any other non-zero exit. A usage limit, an API overload, or a network error stops the chain, the run is pushed, snapshotted, rated, and scored like any early stop, and the manifest records only how many invocations were made. There is no retry, no void, and no separate class or cause anywhere in the record. Nothing is added to the harness or the run procedure, and every run that starts ends as exactly one scored result, so no run is selected away and the run count per scenario never depends on how the infrastructure behaved. Scores measure the account and the network as well as the approach: Cairn's chains spend the most tokens and so stop most often on the usage limit (docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md already tells a user to re-run complete-all-tasks after the window resets), so the delivery the benchmark exists to measure is the one most biased against, and nothing in the record lets a reader see it.

The harness classifies how each invocation ends (completed, the model's own stop, or infrastructure failure with its cause: usage limit, overload, network) from the invocation's JSON result and stderr, and writes the class into the invocation record and an infrastructure-stop field of the manifest. The chain still stops at the failure and the run is still rated and scored as an early stop with no retry and no void; the README reports, beside each scenario's scores, how many of its runs ended on an infrastructure failure. Keeps the draft's every-run-counts scoring and its simple run procedure while making the bias visible, so a reader can discount a scenario whose score is pulled down by infrastructure stops, and the record later supports a different policy without re-running anything. The scores themselves stay biased against the heaviest delivery, and a disclosed count does not say how much each stop cost, so the ranking still orders scenarios partly by how often they met the usage limit; the classification also needs a dependable signal for each failure cause in the host's output.

The harness classifies each invocation's end as in the previous options; on the first infrastructure failure it stops the chain, records the run with its outputs and a void marker naming the failure and the invocation it hit, and excludes it from rating, scoring, and the published pages. A voided run is never a phase-2 parent, and a fresh run of the same scenario (from the same parent for phase 2) is drawn in its place. Nothing is retried, and the voided run's tokens stay in its own record and enter no scenario total. Every scored run is one uninterrupted chain exactly as its delivery states, with no harness-authored message, no re-executed invocation, and no mid-chain state to reason about, so the policy is simple to state and to audit. Survivorship: a run that spends more tokens is likelier to be voided, so the scored runs of a heavy scenario lean toward its cheaper, shorter runs, and a Cairn chain under a subscription usage window may void again and again, paying a whole chain's tokens each time before it ever completes.

The harness classifies each invocation's end; on an infrastructure failure it waits (a short backoff for an overload or network error, until the account's usage window resets for a usage limit, the wait excluded from the run's duration) and resumes the same session by its id under the same pair and flags with one fixed continuation message, up to a fixed number of attempts per invocation, then continues the chain. Every attempt is recorded in the invocation's record with its failure cause and counted in the run's token totals; the manifest counts the retries. An invocation still failing after the last attempt voids the run as in "Void and replace the run". Mirrors how Cairn is actually run (wait out the window, continue) while keeping the session's own context, so a failure in the middle of a multi-step invocation, such as an answer sweep's batched call, picks up where it stopped rather than restarting on a half-changed tree. Adds a harness-authored message to the session that is part of no delivery, so a resumed run did not receive exactly its delivery's inputs, and the fixed message must read the same to every scenario; waits for a usage window can hold a run open for hours, and scored runs still carry the tokens their failed attempts spent.

The harness classifies each invocation's end; on an infrastructure failure it waits as in "Resume the failed session" and runs the same delivery message again as a fresh invocation on the work tree exactly as the failed attempt left it (no reset, no resume), up to a fixed number of attempts, then continues the chain. Every attempt is recorded with its cause and counted in the token totals; an invocation still failing after the last attempt voids the run as in "Void and replace the run". Every message any session receives is still one of its delivery's own lines, so no harness-authored input enters a run, and it matches the documented usage of re-running complete-all-tasks after the window resets, which Cairn's per-task commits and continue-not-redo completion are built for. A fresh process meets the failed attempt's leftovers with no memory of them: Cairn's answer sweep stops on `dirty before start` when a fold was left uncommitted, and a manual delivery's single build message re-run on a half-built tree may restart or duplicate work, so the retry's outcome depends on how each delivery tolerates partial state, which differs by scenario.

Scenario invocations run under pay-per-use API billing rather than a subscription account, so no usage window exists and the usage-limit class of failure does not arise. The remaining overload and network failures are classified and recorded in the invocation record and manifest, and the run is still stopped, rated, and scored as an early stop, with no retry and no void. Removes the dominant cause of the bias, the one that grows with the tokens a delivery spends, at the account rather than in harness logic, so the run procedure keeps its every-run-counts rule with only a classification added and no run waits hours on a window. Every run is paid at API rates rather than inside a subscription, which raises the campaign's money cost by the full token bill; and the residual overload and network failures still count as results, so a transient outage during a long Cairn chain still lowers its score.

Scenario invocations run under pay-per-use API billing, so no usage window exists and usage-limit failures do not arise; any remaining infrastructure failure (overload, network) is classified, stops the chain, and voids the run as in "Void and replace the run", with a fresh run of the same scenario drawn in its place and no retry. Scored runs are free of infrastructure effects with the simplest harness logic: the frequent, token-proportional failure is removed at the source, and the rare transient ones are voided, so survivorship bias stays small and no harness-authored message or re-executed invocation enters any run. Carries the full API-rate cost of every run, voided ones included, and a voided run's spend is pure loss; a sustained provider outage still voids runs in a row, and the policy depends on the benchmark having a billed account to run under.

open-question.question: No scenario invocation carries a time or turn limit while the rater has one, so a runaway session can hold a run open indefinitely. Does each invocation get a time or turn limit, and how is an invocation that hits it classified?
open-question.alternative: Scenario invocations keep running with no time, turn, or spend limit, per invocation or per run, as the draft's one-run procedure now stands. A session ends only by itself or by a failed call, its wall-clock duration is recorded in the manifest as today, and no limit-hit end class exists. Adds no parameter to the design and cuts no scenario short. A slow invocation, most likely Cairn's long task-completion line, can never be stopped by a ceiling set too low, so no score depends on where the ceiling was set. A runaway or hung session holds its run, and any campaign waiting behind it, open indefinitely. The only way to end it is a person killing the process, which breaks the draft's rule that nothing about a run is done by hand, and the kill leaves an end that no rule classifies.

The harness kills each claude -p process after a fixed wall-clock ceiling. This covers the first-form invocation and each operator-reply resume, each process timed on its own. The ceiling is set generously, well above the longest normal invocation (for example a stated multiple of a pilot's longest), and declared as a shared input of the comparison set. A kill stops the chain and is recorded in the manifest as its own end class (time limit). The run is then scored like any other early stop: a result, rated on the tree it left. Bounds every run with one harness-side mechanism that needs no host flag and catches hangs as well as loops. It rarely binds, so it does not shape scores, and it fits the draft's existing rule that an early stop is a result, not a failed measurement. Wall-clock time also depends on API speed and the network, so a hit can come from a stalled connection rather than the model, and counting it as a result scores an outside slowdown against the scenario. Cairn's long invocations are the most exposed to this.

The same generous per-process wall-clock ceiling, declared as a shared input of the comparison set and enforced by the harness, but a kill is classified as an infrastructure failure, not a behavioural stop. It is recorded under that end class and handled by whatever the benchmark does with infrastructure failures, so it is not scored as the scenario's result. A scenario is not penalised for a session held open by something outside the model, such as a stalled API or network. That keeps the bias the gaps report raises (Cairn, the heaviest spender, being the likeliest to hit external limits) out of the scores. A genuine model runaway, such as a loop that never converges, also gets treated as an infrastructure failure, which hides a real behavioural failure mode and can reward it with a retry. What a hit costs depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

alternative.id: Spend or turn cap as result

open-question.alternative: Each invocation runs under a fixed cap the host enforces in the model's own terms: a dollar budget (claude -p's --max-budget-usd) or a cap on agentic turns where the host offers one. The cap is set generously and declared as a shared input of the comparison set, and there is no wall-clock ceiling. Reaching the cap is a behavioural early stop, recorded in the manifest under a limit end class and rated on the tree left. A cap counted in spend or turns does not depend on API or network speed, so a hit always reflects what the model did. Classifying it as a result is then sound. It is also one parameter that is easy to state and to reproduce. It does not bound a hang that spends nothing, such as a stalled connection or a blocked tool call, so the indefinitely-open run the question raises remains possible. It also depends on a host flag whose scope over dispatched subagents must be confirmed, and that flag is recorded per host rather than enforced by the harness.

Two generous limits per claude -p process, both declared as shared inputs of the comparison set. The first is a host-enforced spend or turn cap; reaching it is a behavioural early stop, recorded and rated on the tree left. The second is a harness wall-clock ceiling set above anything the spend cap allows in normal operation; a kill there is classified as an infrastructure failure and handled by the infrastructure-failure policy. The manifest records which limit ended the invocation. Sorts the two ways a session runs away by mechanism, not by judgment: a model that keeps working hits the spend cap and is scored, and a session that stalls hits the clock and is not. This bounds every run without scoring outside slowdowns against a scenario. Two parameters to set, declare, and justify instead of one, plus a dependence on a host flag whose coverage of subagents must be confirmed. Handling of the clock hit depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

A deliberately tight per-invocation limit, in time or spend, that is the same for every scenario and chosen to bind rather than to catch only runaways. Reaching it is an early stop rated on the tree left, so the benchmark measures quality reached within a fixed resource budget. Answers the question of which approach does best when given the same resources, a comparison a reader can take at face value without weighing cost separately. Turns the cost the draft reports beside quality into a constraint on quality. The draft states that Cairn is expected to cost more and that the benchmark reports by how much, so this would systematically cut Cairn's heaviest lines short and score that against it, and the scores would then depend on where the budget was set.

A single wall-clock ceiling on the whole run (every invocation, reply, and operator turn of one prompt's chain), declared as a shared input of the comparison set, with no per-invocation limit. When the deadline passes the harness kills the running process and stops the chain. The run is recorded with a deadline end class and rated on the tree left as an early stop. One number bounds every run's total duration, and with it the length of a campaign, without having to size a ceiling for each kind of invocation. Chains differ greatly in length, from the single manual message to Cairn's eleven or more lines, so one deadline either binds Cairn or is slack for manual. It also lets a runaway early invocation use up the time of every later line, so the stop shows up at a line that did nothing wrong.

open-question.question: A new rating writes new browser tests for every checklist line, so two ratings of one artifact can test the same line at different strictness, and the draft's claim that a second rating gets the same number holds only for re-running an existing test. What must a rater version pass before it may rate a comparison set, and what is the acceptance rule?
open-question.alternative: No calibration gate: a rater version may rate a comparison set as soon as it is defined, with no reference artifacts and no acceptance rule. The draft drops "a second rating of the same artifact gets the same number" and states only what holds, that re-running a rating's committed tests reproduces its verdicts, and leaves the variation between fresh ratings to whatever the sibling questions on repeat-rating agreement and per-line test specifications settle. This is meant as never, not later. No reference artifacts to build or keep in step with each prompt version, and no extra rater runs, so the design stays as small as it is now and stops claiming a property it has not measured. A rater version that writes weak tests (an undo button exists rather than the award being reversed) is caught by nothing before its verdicts reach the published scores, and its strictness differs between rater versions with no shared yardstick. How much noise is left depends on the repeat-rating and line-specification axes the sibling questions own.

A calibration set per prompt version is a shared input: one reference artifact that meets every checklist line, plus deliberately broken variants, each built to fail a known set of lines, so that every test line is failed by at least one variant. Each reading line gets reference items whose verdicts are clear-cut. Every artifact has a recorded verdict for every line. The set is frozen beside the checklist version a comparison set uses. Before it may rate that set, a rater version rates every calibration artifact once through the normal rating path, writing fresh tests that the harness runs. The acceptance rule is exact: every verdict must match the recorded one, and a not-proved verdict counts as a mismatch. A single mismatch refuses the version, which is changed (guideline, model, effort, or budget) and calibrated again as a new rater version. The calibration ratings and their tests are committed as the version's evidence. It catches the failure the question names: a weak test passes on the variant built to fail it, so a rater that tests the same line too leniently cannot rate anything. The rule has one answer and needs no judgment, like every other check in the design. Building a correct reference and enough broken variants for every line of both prompts is substantial work that must be redone whenever a checklist changes. One pass shows that the version can be accurate, not that two fresh ratings agree. A rule with zero tolerance may never be met by a model writing new tests, which would stall every comparison set. How reachable it is depends on whether checklist lines carry test specifications, an axis a sibling question owns.

The same frozen calibration set per prompt version, with a known verdict on every line and a not-proved verdict counted as a mismatch. Before it may rate a comparison set, a rater version rates every calibration artifact a declared number of times (more than one, for example three), each time as an independent rating with fresh tests. The acceptance rule is exact on every repetition: every verdict of every rating matches the recorded one. Any mismatch refuses the version. All repetitions and their tests are committed as evidence. It tests the claim the draft makes, that a second fresh rating gets the same number, against known answers before any score depends on it. It catches both a lenient test and one that is strict in some ratings and lenient in others, which a single pass can miss. The calibration cost is multiplied by the repetition count, and a zero-tolerance rule over several independent ratings is the hardest of all to meet, so a merely good rater version is the most likely to be refused here. It also builds and maintains the whole reference and variant set. Its reachability depends on the line-specification axis a sibling question owns.

The same frozen calibration set per prompt version, with known verdicts on every line. A rater version rates it a declared number of times (one or more) and passes when its agreement with the recorded verdicts reaches a minimum the draft states, for example per axis, with a not-proved verdict counted as a disagreement. Below the minimum the version is refused. A version that passes publishes its agreement figures and every mismatched line beside the comparison set's results. It is a gate that a capable model writing fresh tests can actually pass, while still stopping a rater version that is clearly too lenient or too erratic. Publishing the mismatches shows a reader how much of a score's line count to trust. The tolerated mismatch rate is rater noise that enters every published score and the lost count. The threshold is a number the design has no principled source for. It still carries the cost of building and maintaining the reference and variant set.

The same frozen calibration set per prompt version, with known verdicts on every line, rated by each rater version a declared number of times before or alongside a comparison set. No acceptance rule refuses the version. Its agreement with the recorded verdicts, and the lines it got wrong, are reported beside the comparison set's scores the way the not-proved count is. No comparison set is ever blocked by a rater version that narrowly fails, yet every reader sees how far the rater that produced a score reproduces known verdicts, using the same mechanism the draft already uses for the not-proved count. A demonstrably lenient rater version still produces published scores and ranks, so the reported figure explains noise after the fact rather than keeping it out. The question asks what a rater must pass, and this answers that it passes nothing.

The calibration set is real artifacts from pilot runs of the scenarios rather than purpose-built ones. The maintainer plays each one by hand and records a verdict on every checklist line, and the items and verdicts are frozen as a shared input beside the checklist version. A rater version rates the set before it may rate a comparison set, with a not-proved verdict counted as a mismatch. The acceptance rule is exact. A mismatch is checked by playing the artifact again: if the recorded verdict was wrong, it is corrected as a new calibration-set version; otherwise the rater version is refused. The rater is calibrated on the structural variety real runs produce (multi-file layouts, unusual controls, partial features), which a reference and its variants written by one person do not show. No variants need to be engineered. The known verdicts come from a person's judgment, which the design otherwise keeps out of every number. Lines that no pilot artifact happens to fail have no failing case, so a lenient test on them is never caught. Settling mismatches puts a hand step into the gate.

No known verdicts: the calibration set is a fixed, frozen set of artifacts, such as pilot or earlier-run artifacts. A rater version rates each of them twice, with fresh tests each time, before it may rate a comparison set. The acceptance rule is agreement between its own two ratings, line by line, at a stated minimum or exactly. Below that the version is refused. Nothing needs a reference artifact, broken variants, or hand verdicts, so it is the cheapest gate to set up and keep current across prompt versions. It measures the instability between fresh ratings that the draft's "same number" claim leaves unmeasured. Two ratings that are equally lenient agree perfectly, so the weak-test failure the question opens with passes the gate unseen. It also partly overlaps the repeat-rating agreement on comparison-set artifacts, which a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: The lost count compares two independent ratings, the parent's and the child's, so rater noise shows as lines lost or gained when nothing changed, and no agreement figure is reported anywhere. Is a sample of each comparison set's artifacts rated twice with the agreement reported beside the scores, and at what sample size?
open-question.alternative: No artifact is rated twice and no agreement figure is computed. The draft's claim under "The axes" that a second rating of the same artifact gets the same number is narrowed to re-running a committed test, and the lost count is described as a tally that includes rater noise, a lost line being a pointer to the run record and never evidence on its own. Rater variability is left to whatever the rater version must pass before rating and to how precisely each checklist line is specified. Costs no extra rater run and adds nothing to the harness, the rating file, the analysis, or the page, while making the draft stop claiming a repeatability nobody measured. The lost count, the number phase 2 is expected to show Cairn's margin on, stays uninterpretable: a reader cannot tell whether a mean of two lost lines is behaviour or noise, and a rater version that drifts between ratings goes unnoticed. How much this costs depends on how strict the sibling rater calibration gate and checklist line specifications turn out to be.

The harness re-rates a fixed number of randomly chosen artifacts per prompt in each comparison set (for example five), as a fresh blind rating under the same rater version, the rater not told it is a repeat. Scores and the lost count use the first rating only. The analysis output reports the per-line verdict agreement (the share of lines with the same verdict in both ratings) and the per-axis score difference for the sample; the README page carries nothing new. Gives a developer a measured noise floor for every comparison set at a small, fixed rater cost that does not grow with the scenario roster or the number of runs. A sample this small yields a wide estimate and may miss the artifacts hardest to rate (a canvas UI, an unusual entry structure), and a reader of the page, where the ranking and the lost column are read, never sees the figure.

One randomly chosen run of every scenario, for each prompt, is re-rated blind under the same rater version, so the sample grows with the roster; scores use the first rating only. The per-line verdict agreement and the per-axis score difference are reported in one line beside the README ranking table, and the lost column carries a noise floor beside the mean lost count: the expected number of lines lost by rater disagreement alone, computed from the rate at which a line passing in one rating of an artifact fails in the other. No threshold is applied; a low agreement is published as it is. Puts the noise figure where the scores and the lost count are read, so a reader compares the lost count to what noise alone produces, and every scenario contributes, so an artifact style one delivery tends to produce cannot escape the sample. Rater cost grows with the roster, one repeat per scenario per prompt still gives a coarse per-scenario estimate, and the page gains one more figure to explain. Its size depends on the sibling scenario roster and runs-per-scenario decisions.

The per-scenario repeat sample and the page reporting of the per-scenario option, plus a declared minimum agreement (for example a per-line verdict agreement under which the set fails) that is part of the rater definition. A comparison set whose sample falls below it is not complete: its page is not regenerated, and it is rated again under a revised rater version. Turns the agreement figure into a guarantee: no comparison set reaches the page with a rater whose ratings demonstrably did not reproduce on that set's own artifacts, which a calibration set of reference artifacts cannot show. The threshold is a number nobody can derive and must be argued for, a failing set costs a full re-rating and can stall a campaign, and the gate overlaps the sibling rater calibration gate, so its value depends on what that gate already requires before a rater version may rate.

Every run id gets two independent blind ratings under the same rater version. A line's score is the mean of its two verdicts, the agreement per scenario and per axis is reported beside the scores on the page, and a prompt-1 line counts as lost only when both ratings of the parent pass it and both ratings of the child fail it. Halves the effect of single-rating noise on every score and makes the lost count robust by construction, with an agreement figure for every scenario rather than an estimate from a sample. Doubles the rating cost and time of every comparison set and of every development check, which the fast loop under "How Cairn development uses the benchmark" was built to keep at one rater run per candidate commit, and a line with split verdicts scores a half that no test can re-derive.

No random sample is drawn. Every line the analysis sorts as lost (and as gained) between a parent and its child is re-rated afresh on both artifacts, with a new test for that line only, and counts as lost only when the re-rating confirms both verdicts. The confirmation rate is reported beside the lost count; the axis scores carry no agreement figure. Spends rater runs only on the number the question names, so the published lost count holds only differences that reproduced, at a cost proportional to how many lines changed rather than to the size of the set. Measures noise only where a verdict already changed, so a line falsely kept or falsely failed on both artifacts is never caught, the confirmation re-rating removes false losses without finding missed ones, and the axis scores, which rank the scenarios, get no noise figure at all.

The per-scenario repeat sample with its agreement line and noise floor beside the README table, and in addition the targeted re-rating of every lost and gained line on both parent and child, a line counting as lost only when the re-rating confirms it. Covers both halves of the problem: the axis scores get a measured agreement figure on the page, and the lost count is both confirmed line by line and set against a noise floor. The most harness and analysis work of any partial option, two separate repeat mechanisms to specify and keep in step, and a rater cost that grows with both the roster and the number of changed lines; its size depends on the sibling scenario roster and runs-per-scenario decisions.

open-question.question: Each checklist line names a behaviour and nothing more, so a weak test (an undo button exists) and a strict one (the award is actually reversed) both satisfy it. Does each line carry a short specification of the case its test must drive and what it must assert?
open-question.alternative: Every test line (prompt 1's six stated and thirteen implied lines, prompt 2's stated line and eleven implied lines, and prompt 2's carry-between-profiles hidden line) gets a short specification written now into the draft's project section beside the line. The specification names the case the test must drive the artifact into and the observable outcome it must assert, stated as an outcome rather than a means, so the "any way through counts" rule still holds: for the award line, award a point, take it back, and assert the score is back to its earlier value, with a confirmation that prevents the award counting as well. The specification becomes part of the checklist, which stays derived from the draft and nothing else, and keeps the line's id. Pins the strictness of every test line at the one source the checklist is already derived from, so two ratings of one artifact test the same case with the same assertion and the specs are reviewed in the open within this milestone. Roughly thirty-two specs have to be written and agreed now, which lengthens the project section considerably, and an outcome stated too narrowly can fail a legitimate way through that the line's wording meant to accept.

alternative.id: Spec form in draft, specs at implementation

open-question.alternative: The draft adds the rule that every test line carries a specification of the case to drive and the outcome to assert, gives its form and one or two worked examples, and changes the derivation rule so the checklist is the draft's lines plus specifications authored in the benchmark repository's inputs area when the checklist is first built. The per-line specifications are not written in this milestone. Settles the design point (each line carries a spec) within the milestone's goal of finalizing the draft, without writing every spec before the harness, the rater, and an artifact to try them on exist. The checklist stops being derived from the draft alone, and until the specs are written nothing pins strictness; whether they are fixed before scored runs depends on the input-freeze question.

The checklist lines stay behaviour-only as the draft has them; each test line's specification of the case to drive and the outcome to assert lives in the rater definition, beside its fixed rating guideline, so it is part of the rater version that every rating file names and the analysis groups by. A sharpened or corrected spec is a new rater version, never a change to the checklist, so line ids and the checklist's derivation stay untouched and ratings made under different specs never mix. What a line means is split across two inputs, and a spec change regroups every earlier rating under an older rater version rather than being re-rated against the same checklist; how a rater version is gated depends on the rater-calibration question.

Only the test lines where a weak and a strict test plainly diverge (an award taken back, a reload surviving, a skip keeping its place, a tie settled, edits not lost, the carry between profiles) get a short case-and-assertion specification in the draft's project section; the remaining lines stay behaviour-only. Spends the writing where the variance actually arises and keeps lines whose test has one obvious form, such as the file opening from disk, as short as they are. Choosing which lines are ambiguous is itself a judgment, so a weak test the selection did not foresee still passes on an unspecified line.

alternative.id: One strictness rule in the guideline

open-question.alternative: No per-line specification. The rater's fixed rating guideline gains one general rule applied to every test line: a test must drive the artifact into the case the line names and assert the resulting state, never only the presence of a control, label, or button. Closes the named failure (a test that only finds an undo button) with one sentence that also covers lines added later, at no cost to the checklist's length. Leaves to each rating what the resulting state is for each line, so two strict tests can still assert different outcomes and disagree on the same artifact.

Nothing is added to the checklist lines or the rating guideline; a line keeps naming a behaviour only, and variance in test strictness is left to be caught by whatever checks of the rater the benchmark adopts. Keeps the checklist exactly as short and as derivable as it is now, and adds no input to write, freeze, or version. Two ratings of one artifact can still test a line at different strictness, which also shows as lost or gained lines in phase 2 when nothing changed; whether that is caught at all depends on the rater-calibration and repeat-rating questions.

open-question.question: A test line the rater could not drive the artifact to scores zero like a missing behaviour, with the not-proved count reported beside the axis, which penalises an artifact a browser test finds hard to drive (a canvas-based UI) regardless of what a host could do with it. open-question.question: The define line records "Carry out the task described in PROJECT.md." verbatim as milestone 1's goal, and phase 2 overwrites that file, so from then on the recorded goal points at prompt 2 and the phase-2 starting-state pass reads a milestone whose goal no longer describes what it built. Nothing in the harness, the delivery lists, the no-prompt-text rule, or Cairn changes. Every delivery keeps one identical fixed first message with no exception to the rule that no message carries prompt text, nothing in a delivery knows which phase it runs in, and Cairn needs no change. The phase-2 starting-state pass, the step the draft names as the main source of Cairn's expected phase-2 margin, reads a closed milestone whose goal now describes the wrong request, both milestones get the same content-free goal and a slug from "Carry out the task described", and the chain does not use Cairn the way a real project does, where a goal holds content.

alternative.id: Prompt text in cairn define line

Each milestone's recorded goal is the request it was opened for and stays true after the file is overwritten, the slug and title come from real content, and no scenario gains information, since every manual run finds the same text in the same committed file. The cairn define line becomes the one planned message whose text varies by phase, so the delivery is no longer a purely fixed list and the model-strategy row for the define line must match it by prefix; the prompt also reaches the cairn chain through the command line as well as the file, a channel asymmetry the draft must argue is harmless (neither prompt holds a double quote today, but a future prompt that did would break the quoting rule).

It reverses the draft's deliberate choice that the agent finds the task in the repository the way a developer would, changes every scenario rather than only the one that drifts, gives manual runs the prompt twice (message and file), and makes every delivery's first message phase-dependent.

Cairn's define-milestone-goal gains a form that takes the goal from a named file and records that file's content at define time under `## Goal`, with its docs and skill reference updated, hosts rebuilt, and both test runs green; the define line becomes one fixed message naming PROJECT.md through that form, identical in both phases, and no message carries prompt text. The recorded goal holds the prompt's content and stays true after phase 2 overwrites the file, while the delivery list stays fixed, phase-blind, and free of any exception to the no-prompt-text rule. It adds an argument surface to a Cairn skill chiefly to serve the benchmark, the chain then exercises a define path the usage documentation's chains do not use, and the result depends on a Cairn release the benchmark's earlier version deliveries (such as 1.8.3) lack.

The define line keeps a pointer rather than content, but one that cannot move: it names the prompt as committed in the phase's own `Prompt: <n>` commit (for example "Carry out the task described in PROJECT.md as committed in Prompt: 2."), so each milestone's goal points at a fixed point in history; PROJECT.md is still overwritten and no message carries prompt text. The recorded goal stays accurate for the life of the run with no prompt text in any message and no change to Cairn. The define message differs by phase, breaking the rule that nothing in a delivery knows which phase it runs in, the goal still holds no content so every reader (the starting-state pass, a later review) must resolve it through git history, and the line names a harness commit convention that real Cairn use never has.

Every recorded pointer stays true without putting prompt text in any message or changing Cairn, and the deliveries stay symmetric across manual and cairn. Prompt 1 stays readable in the phase-2 tree rather than only in history, which changes what every phase-2 run sees against the draft's "no restatement" second request, the pointer sentence becomes phase-dependent in every delivery, and the goal still holds a pointer rather than content.

open-question.question: Phase 1 is run for every scenario "as many times as the set calls for", with no number set and no stopping rule, so a margin between two scenarios can be noise. How many runs per scenario does a comparison set require?
open-question.alternative: The draft fixes the count at one phase-1 run per scenario of a comparison set, for every scenario alike, with phase 2 run once from it as now; the runs column then always reads 1 and a margin is read as a single observation. Cheapest complete set: every scenario costs one chain per phase, the same unit as the development fast loop, so a full set (the Cairn chains being the costliest and likeliest to hit usage limits) stays affordable and finishes soonest. Gives no spread at all, so no margin between two scenarios can be told from noise and the hidden axis (two pass-or-fail checks per run) swings by a whole third of the overall score on one run; it resolves the gap only by stating that the page's ranking is anecdotal.

The draft fixes the count at three phase-1 runs per scenario for every scenario of a comparison set, declared before the set's first scored run with no stopping rule, each with its own phase-2 child, so every row rests on three runs per prompt. The smallest count that yields a median and a range per score, so a spread can stand beside each cell and a run that went off the rails cannot alone decide a rank, at three times the cost of a single run. Three runs give only a rough spread: an interval from three points is wide, so most margins between close scenarios still come out unresolved, and a binary-heavy axis like hidden moves in thirds; what the spread is and how ties are called are the spread-reporting and tie-threshold questions' to settle.

The draft fixes the count at five phase-1 runs per scenario for every scenario of a comparison set, declared before the set's first scored run with no stopping rule, each with its own phase-2 child. Enough runs for an interval narrow enough to separate a moderate margin, such as Cairn rows against the best manual row, while keeping a set within a few days of runs.
