Five times the single-run cost on every scenario, the Cairn chains and their usage-limit exposure included, and still too few to resolve small margins or to estimate the hidden axis finer than in fifths.

The draft fixes the count at ten phase-1 runs per scenario for every scenario of a comparison set, declared before the set's first scored run with no stopping rule, each with its own phase-2 child. Gives intervals tight enough that small margins and per-axis differences, the hidden axis included, can be read as findings rather than noise, which is what the page's claim that several Cairn rows stand above the best manual row needs. Ten full chains per phase per scenario make a set cost roughly ten times a single pass and take many days, which multiplies the infrastructure-failure and CLI-version drift a long campaign meets and puts the release gate's slow loop further out of reach.

The draft fixes a stopping rule instead of a number: every scenario starts with a declared minimum (three runs), and further phase-1 runs, each with its phase-2 child, are added to the scenarios whose margin to an adjacent ranked row is still unresolved until it resolves or a declared cap (such as ten) is reached; minimum, cap, and rule are declared before the set's first scored run, and scenarios may end with different run counts. Spends runs only where a margin is close, so clearly separated scenarios stay cheap and close ones get the resolution they need, with the stopping rule fixed in advance rather than left to the maintainer. Adaptive stopping inflates false separations unless the rule corrects for it, unequal counts complicate the table and when a set counts as complete, and the rule depends on how the spread is computed and what counts as a tie, which the spread-reporting and tie-threshold questions own.

The draft fixes a uniform count for the scenarios that appear on the page (the four primary deliveries), declared before the set's first scored run and no fewer than three, with no stopping rule, while ablation deliveries and candidate-commit scenarios, which appear only in the analysis output, run once each. Concentrates the cost on the rows the published ranking and radar rest on, while the ablation and candidate runs stay at the fast loop's one-run price that the development uses already assume. Ablation and candidate comparisons inherit no spread, so a single-run result can still mislead a development decision, and the rule needs a stated boundary of which scenarios are primary, which depends on the roster the scenario-roster question owns.

The draft fixes no number but requires every comparison set to declare its run count per scenario (uniform across the set's scenarios, at least two) in the set's definition before its first scored run, recorded beside the set's other versioned inputs, so later runs cannot be added after results are seen. Closes the stopping-rule hole, the count being fixed before any result can influence it, while leaving each set free to match its count to its budget and purpose. Different sets can carry different counts, so the trend across sets mixes rows of unequal precision, and the draft still says nothing about what count makes a margin meaningful; whether the declaration rides in the set's definition depends on the comparison-set-definition question.

The draft keeps "as many times as the set calls for" with no number and no stopping rule, the gap rejected with the reason stated in the text: the runs column already shows how many runs stand behind each row, and noise is left to whatever spread and tie handling the page reports. Commits no budget and no statistical design before a single run exists, so the first sets can be run at whatever count the maintainer can afford and the number chosen later from observed variance. Leaves optional stopping open, since runs can be added until a margin looks right, and a margin between two scenarios stays possibly noise unless the spread-reporting and tie-threshold questions supply what this count would have.

open-question.question: The ranking table has a runs column but no spread or interval beside any score, so a reader cannot tell a margin between two scenarios from noise. Is a per-run spread or interval reported beside every score, and where?
open-question.alternative: No spread or interval is reported anywhere: the ranking table keeps its runs column as the only sign of how many runs stand behind a row, the analysis output carries means only, and the radar draws means only. The draft states that a margin between two rows carries no measure of its noise, and leaves handling noise, if at all, to how many runs a set requires and to how the rank treats near-equal scores. Keeps the table at its twelve columns and the analysis at one number per cell, and adds no statistic whose meaning at a small run count would itself need explaining. Leaves the gap exactly as the report found it: a reader still cannot tell a margin from noise, and the page's headline reading (several Cairn rows above the best manual row) rests on means of unstated variability; whether that is tolerable depends on the axes the runs-per-scenario and rank-tie siblings settle.

Each score cell of the README ranking table (overall, the three axes, and the lost count) carries the minimum and maximum over the scenario's runs beside its mean, written in the cell as, for example, 82 (76–88), each run counted as one phase-1 run with its phase-2 child, whose two prompt scores are averaged as the scenario mean is; the analysis output carries the same ranges and every run's individual scores. Cost, time, invocations, and sessions stay means without spread, and the radar draws means only. A descriptive range needs no distributional assumption, is honest at any run count of two or more, and puts the variability on the landing page in the same cell a reader is already comparing, with no new column. A range says how far runs scattered, not whether two means differ, so overlapping ranges are read as a tie by eye with no stated rule, and the range widens with every added run; a row resting on one run shows no range at all, which depends on the run count the runs-per-scenario sibling sets.

As the range option, the minimum and maximum over the scenario's runs written in the cell beside each mean, but on every numeric cell of the README ranking table: the overall, the three axes, and the lost count, and also cost in dollars, wall-clock time, and attentive sessions; invocations made over planned stays as it is, and the radar draws means only. The analysis output carries the same ranges and every run's individual values. Puts cost and time under the same scrutiny as quality, so the page's rule that a quality win is read beside its cost holds for the cost's variability too, which matters most for Cairn, whose long chains are where a runaway or retried run inflates one run's cost. Every cell of an already twelve-column table doubles in width, and the cost spread answers a question the report did not raise; it shares the range option's limits, a range that is not a test and empty at one run, the latter depending on the runs-per-scenario sibling.

Each score cell of the README ranking table (overall, the three axes, and the lost count) carries a 95% confidence interval on its mean beside the mean, computed over the scenario's runs (each a phase-1 run with its phase-2 child), by a method the draft names once (a bootstrap over runs or a t-interval); the analysis output carries the same intervals and every run's individual scores. Cost and time stay means, and the radar draws means only. An interval on the mean speaks to the question the reader actually has, how precisely each row's score is known, and two rows whose intervals do not overlap differ by more than noise under a conservative reading. At the small run counts an expensive Cairn chain affords, a t-interval is very wide and a bootstrap over a handful of runs is unstable or degenerate, so the method and a minimum run count must be stated, which ties this option to the runs-per-scenario sibling; overlapping per-row intervals also understate significance compared with an interval on the difference.

The per-score premise is rejected: instead of a spread beside each score, the README ranking table gains one column holding, for every row, the difference between its overall score and the overall of a stated reference row (the best manual row) with a 95% interval on that difference over the two scenarios' runs; the per-axis differences with their intervals, and every run's individual scores, go in the analysis output. The score cells and the radar stay means. Answers exactly the comparison the page exists to make, whether a Cairn row stands above the best manual row by more than noise, in one column, with a single interval per row that is tighter and more honest than reading two per-row intervals for overlap. Says nothing about the noise between two Cairn rows or two manual rows, ties the column's meaning to which row is the reference, and needs the same minimum run count and named method as any interval, depending on the runs-per-scenario sibling.

Only the overall score cell of the README ranking table carries the spread beside its mean (the minimum and maximum over the scenario's runs, each a phase-1 run with its phase-2 child); the three axis cells, the lost count, cost, and time stay means on the page, and the analysis output carries the spread of every score and every run's individual scores. The radar draws means only. Shows the variability of the one number the rank orders by, where a reader's ordering judgment is made, while keeping the table nearly as compact as it is now. The axis cells, where the expected gain sits (the hidden axis rests on two checks per run and is the noisiest), stay bare on the page, so the per-axis reading the radar invites is still made without any measure of noise; a range is also empty at one run, depending on the runs-per-scenario sibling.

The README ranking table stays as it is, means and the runs column, with one line under it linking the analysis output; the analysis output carries every run's individual scores per scenario and, beside every mean, both its minimum-to-maximum range and its 95% confidence interval over the scenario's runs. The radar draws means only. Keeps the landing page compact and readable while putting the full record a careful reader needs one link away, with the raw per-run values that let them compute any statistic of their own. The reader the page is written for, who reads the table and leaves, still cannot tell a margin from noise on the page itself, and a headline of Cairn rows standing above manual ones is shown without the qualification that might undo it; the interval's usefulness depends on the runs-per-scenario sibling.

open-question.question: The rank orders scenarios by overall score and breaks ties by cost, with no threshold below which two scores count as equal, so a difference within noise still orders two rows. Is there a margin under which two overall scores tie and cost decides?
open-question.alternative: The rank stays as the draft has it: scenarios are ordered by the exact overall score, only two exactly equal scores tie, and cost breaks such a tie in favour of the cheaper scenario. No margin is declared, and whether a margin between two rows is noise is left to whatever the table reports beside the scores. Nothing new to define, justify, or keep in step: the rank is a total order computed mechanically from the per-axis means, with no constant anyone has to argue for and no grouping rule for chains of near-equal scores. Overall scores are means of fractions, so exact equality practically never occurs and the cost rule is dead text; a difference well inside noise still orders two rows, so the table's intended reading (Cairn rows above the best manual row) can rest on noise, and a reader can tell otherwise only if the table reports a spread, which the Score spread reporting question owns.

Overall scores are compared at the precision the table prints them (for example whole points on the 0 to 100 scale): two scores that print the same tie, and the cheaper scenario ranks higher. No noise-based margin is declared. The rank never contradicts what the reader sees, since two rows showing the same overall are never ordered by an invisible decimal, and the existing cost rule becomes live without introducing a tuned constant. Print precision is a formatting choice, not a noise estimate: differences of a few points, which can still be rater or run noise, keep ordering rows, so the gap the question raises is narrowed only at its smallest end.

Overall scores are compared at the precision the table prints them: two scores that print the same share one rank number and are marked as tied, and their listing order within the tie carries no claim (cost no longer breaks ties). No noise-based margin is declared. Removes the contradiction between the draft's rule that cost is never ranked and its use of cost as a tie-breaker, while keeping the rank consistent with what is printed and adding no constant. Like the other print-precision option it leaves noise-sized differences ordering rows; and a shared top rank within a family leaves the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" ambiguous, which needs a rule from the Radar curve selection question.

The draft declares one fixed margin in points on the 0 to 100 overall score, set before a comparison set's first scored run and versioned with the analysis; two scenarios whose overall scores differ by less than it tie, and the cheaper one ranks higher. Tie groups are formed from the top of the order down, each row joining the group whose top row it is within the margin of, so chains of near-equal scores resolve one way. A quality difference too small to trust can no longer put an expensive scenario above a cheaper one, which is the reading the cost tie-break was written for; the rule is simple, reproducible from the columns, and identical across comparison sets, so ranks under it compare over the trend. The margin's value is chosen before any noise has been measured, so it is a guess that may be too tight to matter or too loose to separate real differences; it brings cost into the rank, against the draft's statement that cost is never ranked, and can lift a cheap manual row above a Cairn row on the page's headline reading.

The draft declares one fixed margin in points on the 0 to 100 overall score, set before a comparison set's first scored run and versioned with the analysis; scenarios whose overall scores fall within it of their group's top row share one rank number and are marked as tied, and cost plays no part in the rank, staying a column the reader weighs. Says exactly what the data supports, that the tied rows are indistinguishable on quality, without the benchmark weighing cost for the reader, which keeps the rank consistent with the draft's rule that cost is never ranked. The margin is still a guess made before noise is measured; tied groups make the table's ordering partly uninformative, and the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" becomes ambiguous within a tied group, which needs a rule from the Radar curve selection question.

The margin is not a constant but is derived per comparison set from the set's own measured noise: two scenarios tie when the difference between their overall scores lies within a declared statistical bound computed from their per-run scores (for example overlapping intervals at a declared level, widened by the rater agreement figure where one is reported), and within a tie the cheaper scenario ranks higher. The bound's formula and level are declared in the draft before the first scored run. A tie means precisely "this difference is within the noise the set actually showed", so the rank tracks the data rather than a guessed constant, and cost decides only where quality genuinely cannot. It exists only if the set carries several runs per scenario and computes a per-run spread, axes owned by the Runs per scenario and Score spread reporting questions (with one run per scenario no bound can be computed); the analysis grows more complex, the threshold moves between comparison sets so ranks are not formed under one rule over the trend, and cost enters the rank against the draft's statement that it is never ranked.

The margin is derived per comparison set from the set's own measured noise, by a declared statistical bound on the difference of two scenarios' per-run overall scores (for example overlapping intervals at a declared level, widened by the rater agreement figure where one is reported); scenarios within it of their group's top row share one rank number and are marked as tied, and cost plays no part in the rank. The most defensible statement the page can make: rows are ordered only where the set's own data separates them, and the benchmark never weighs cost against quality for the reader. Depends on several runs per scenario and a computed spread, owned by the Runs per scenario and Score spread reporting questions; it carries the most analysis machinery, the threshold varies between comparison sets, and with few runs most rows may tie, leaving the table's headline reading and the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" (the Radar curve selection question) without a clear order.

open-question.question: Each family's radar curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the best of several noisy scores is biased upward, more so for Cairn, which has many configurations (versions times strategies) where manual has few. Which scenario is each family's radar curve drawn from?
open-question.alternative: Each family's curve stays drawn from its highest-ranked scenario in the current comparison set's table, as the draft has it, and the gap is rejected in the draft's text with the reason stated: the ranking table lists every rated configuration, so the radar is read as best against best and the table carries the configuration count. Needs no new rule, no extra declaration, and no change to the analysis, and it keeps the draft's reading of every approach at its best configuration and of every radar value as a ranking-table cell. The upward bias of a best-of-several pick stays in the chart and grows with the number of configurations, which favours the Cairn families (and the multi-prompt controls that mirror them) over manual_prompt, so the page's claim of a fair, honest margin rests on a selection known to favour the system it measures.

Each family's curve stays drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the line under the chart that names each curve's scenario also states how many rated configurations it was chosen from, with one sentence in the radar text saying that a best-of pick is biased upward the more configurations stand behind it; the draft's sentence calling the selection fair is rewritten to match. Keeps the draft's selection and every radar value a table cell while removing the unstated part of the bias, so a reader can weigh a Cairn curve chosen from many configurations against a manual one chosen from few. Discloses the bias without reducing it: the curves still overstate the many-configuration families, and the chart, which a reader takes in before the line under it, keeps showing a margin the disclosure itself says is inflated.

One Cairn configuration (a version under a model strategy) is chosen as the one whose cairn scenarios rank highest in the set, and the cairn yolo, cairn assess, and multi-prompt curves are all drawn from that one configuration's three scenarios; the manual_prompt curve is drawn from its own highest-ranked scenario. Makes the gap between the two Cairn curves isolate the stakeholder's turn and the gap to the multi-prompt curve isolate Cairn's structure, as the draft's radar text claims they do, which independent best-of picks across different versions and strategies cannot guarantee, and it replaces three best-of selections over the Cairn configurations with one. Still selects on the same noisy scores it then draws, so the Cairn curves keep an upward bias that grows with the number of configurations, and the multi-prompt curve is no longer that family's best, which can understate the strongest manual-side configuration the draft says Cairn is read against.

Before a comparison set's first scored run, the set's definition names one reference scenario per family (for example both cairn deliveries for the current release under models_strategy_1, the multi-prompt control mirroring that yolo scenario, and one declared manual_prompt pair), and each curve is drawn from its declared scenario whatever the table's ranking turns out to be; every other configuration appears only in the table. Removes the selection bias outright, since nothing about the chart depends on which noisy score came out highest, and fixes the scenarios behind the curves so the two Cairn curves and the multi-prompt curve are matched by construction. The radar no longer shows any family at its best, so a declared manual pair that turns out weaker than another rated manual configuration makes the Cairn margin read against a weak baseline, exactly what the draft wanted to avoid; its worth depends on what the set must hold and how it is declared, an axis the scenario-roster question owns.

The two Cairn curves are drawn from pre-declared reference scenarios named before the set's first scored run (one version under one model strategy), while the manual_prompt and multi-prompt curves are each drawn from their family's highest-ranked scenario in the table. Turns the selection bias against Cairn rather than for it: the Cairn curves carry no best-of inflation while the manual curves keep theirs, so any Cairn margin the chart shows is conservative and the draft's reading against the strongest manual configuration still holds. Mixes two selection rules on one chart, so the gap between curves no longer measures any single comparison, the multi-prompt curve may come from a different configuration than the Cairn curves it is meant to mirror, and a real Cairn margin can be understated or hidden.

Each family's curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario among an equal number of configurations per family, the same count for every family and the configurations in each pool declared before the set's first scored run; a family with more rated configurations than the count draws only from its declared pool. Keeps every family shown at its best and every radar value a table cell while making the best-of bias the same size for every family, so it no longer favours the family with more configurations. Equal bias is not zero bias, so every curve stays inflated relative to a single scenario's true score, and the manual_prompt family must be run under as many strategies as Cairn has configurations in its pool, raising the cost of every set; its viability depends on what the set's roster must hold, an axis the scenario-roster question owns.

Each family's scenario is still chosen as its highest-ranked, but the ranking used for the choice is computed from one fixed half of each scenario's runs (declared before the set, for example the odd-numbered runs) and the curve's values from the other half, so the chosen scenario's drawn scores come from runs that played no part in choosing it. Keeps every family shown at its best configuration while removing the selection bias from the drawn values for every family alike, whatever the number of configurations behind it. Halves the runs behind every drawn value, making each curve noisier, and the drawn values are no longer cells of the ranking table unless the table gains held-out columns, against the draft's rule that nothing depends on the chart; it needs at least two runs per scenario, a count the runs-per-scenario question owns.

No single scenario is chosen: each family's curve is the per-axis mean over every rated scenario of that family in the current comparison set (for the Cairn families, the current version's scenarios across its model strategies), and the line under the chart states how many scenarios each curve averages. Involves no selection at all, so there is no best-of bias, and it matches the ranking table's own stated reading that Cairn wins as a family of configurations rather than as one tuned winner. A curve is no longer any scenario a reader could run, its values are not table cells, and a weak or deliberately exploratory configuration drags its family down, so the curve's height depends on which configurations happened to be rated, an axis the scenario-roster question owns.

open-question.question: The hidden-requirements axis rests on two checks per run (one reading line in phase 1 and one test line in phase 2) yet weighs one third of the overall score, as much as roughly thirty-seven implied lines. Does the hidden axis keep equal weight in the overall score, or is it reported beside an overall computed without it?
open-question.alternative: The overall score stays the unweighted mean of the stated, hidden, and implied axes, and the rank still orders by it. The hidden requirement stays one per prompt, so the axis keeps resting on the phase-1 reading line (a count out of ten) and the phase-2 yes-or-no test line. The draft adds the reason the hidden axis keeps its third despite its two checks, and the ranking table keeps the per-axis columns beside the overall as it does now. It keeps the draft's stated rule that equal weights are the only weights nobody has to argue for, and leaves the axis the question-and-answer loop is tested on at full influence on the rank, where the draft expects Cairn's gain to show. Two checks per run carry as much of the overall as about thirty-seven implied lines, and the phase-2 check is binary, so one run's 0 or 100 on a single test moves the overall by a third of the scale and can reorder the rank on noise; the draft would be keeping, knowingly, the imbalance the design-gaps report raised.

The overall score becomes the unweighted mean of the stated and implied axes only, and the rank orders by that. The hidden axis stays a scored axis in every other place: its own ranking-table column beside the overall, and its axis on the radar. The draft states why the hidden axis is reported beside the rank rather than in it. The rank no longer swings on two checks, and the hidden result is still shown on its own, unblended, where a reader sees the clearest evidence the benchmark produces without it being diluted or amplified by a weighting choice. The one axis designed to show what Cairn's question loop buys stops affecting the rank, so a scenario that never meets a hidden requirement can rank first, and the headline ordering no longer reflects the outcome the benchmark exists to test; a reader must read two numbers to see the comparison the draft frames as its point.

The hidden axis stays in the overall score but at a declared weight below the other two (for example half the weight of each), the overall becoming a weighted mean whose weights the draft states and fixes per comparison set. The hidden column and radar axis stay as they are. The hidden result still bears on the rank, so a scenario that surfaces the hidden requirement is rewarded, while one noisy binary check can no longer move the overall by a full third of the scale. Any weight below a third and above zero is a number someone has to argue for, the very thing the draft's equal-weight rule avoids, and the chosen value is arbitrary with no line-count or evidential basis to anchor it; a later change to it is an analysis version that splits comparisons made before and after it.

The overall score stops being a mean of axis scores and becomes the passing share of every checklist line pooled across axes, each line counting once (a reading line contributing its items' fraction), so each axis weighs in proportion to how many lines it has: the hidden axis about two lines' worth across both prompts, the stated axis its sentences, and the implied axis its roughly thirty-seven lines. The per-axis scores stay in their columns and on the radar. The weights follow mechanically from the checklist with nothing chosen by hand, so each check counts the same and the overall's sensitivity to any one check matches the evidence behind it. It also reweights the stated axis, which the draft calls the floor under the others, down to a handful of lines against the implied list, so the overall becomes mostly an implied-coverage score; the hidden result all but vanishes from the rank, and every later change to an implied list's length silently shifts every axis's weight.

Equal weight is kept, and the premise that the axis rests on two checks is rejected instead: the "one per prompt" rule is replaced by a fixed number of hidden requirements per prompt (several, each with its own seed evidence and check line), so the hidden axis becomes the mean over several checks per prompt like the other axes. It removes the imbalance at its cause rather than by weighting: the axis that tests the question loop keeps its third of the rank while resting on enough checks that one missed requirement no longer swings it. Each extra hidden requirement needs seed evidence calibrated so the prompt gives no reason to ask yet the question settles it, in a small seed README where several planted pieces of evidence can point at each other or at an implied convention; it multiplies the authoring and calibration work, changes the seed and the Closest Wins project section, and depends on whatever calibration procedure the hidden-requirement pilot sets.

The overall score and the rank are dropped: the ranking table shows the three axis scores side by side with no blended number, ordered by a fixed key the draft states (such as delivery family then scenario id), and the radar stays the per-axis comparison. No weight for the hidden axis, or any axis, is set because no axes are combined. No weighting question exists at all, so nothing about the hidden axis's two checks is amplified or buried, and the page shows only numbers each re-derivable from the checklist lines, consistent with the draft's refusal to weigh trade-offs for the reader. The page loses its one-glance answer to which approach is best and the table's reason to order its rows, and the radar's per-family curve is currently chosen by rank, so this depends on how the radar curve selection is settled; the tie-by-cost rule and the "several Cairn rows above the best manual row" reading lose their basis.

open-question.question: A comparison set is one seed tag and one version of each prompt, yet an operator change must also start a new set, the analysis groups by rater version, and the host CLI auto-updates across a campaign that spans several days. Which versions define a comparison set?
open-question.alternative: A comparison set is defined by five versions: the seed tag, one version of each prompt (per phase, as the draft's "One versioning" rule already states), the operator definition, the rater definition, and one exact host CLI version. The host version is pinned: the set declares it, the harness switches off the host's auto-update for the campaign, and the pre-flight refuses a run whose installed host version differs. The rater version is part of the set's identity but the runs are not: a new rater version re-rates the existing runs, and those ratings form a new set over the same runs without re-running any scenario. Every factor the draft already says changes results is held fixed inside a set, so a difference within it can be attributed to the scenario definitions alone, as the draft's attribution rule requires, while a rater fix costs only a re-rating rather than a whole new campaign of Cairn's token-heavy runs. It adds a pinning mechanism and a pre-flight check to the harness, and every host upgrade then starts a new set, so staying on a current host means re-running every scenario; how sets connect across such changes depends on the trend question, and when a set counts as complete depends on the roster question.

A comparison set is defined by the seed tag, one version of each prompt per phase, the operator definition, the rater definition, and one exact host CLI version pinned as above (auto-update off, pre-flight refuses a mismatch). The rater version is bound to the campaign: runs are rated once, under the rater version of the set they were made for, and a new rater version is used only with a fresh set of runs, never to re-rate old ones. A set is one campaign with every version fixed from first run to last rating, which also keeps factors nobody records (server-side model behaviour, the date a run happened) as close together as they can be, and no run ever carries two ratings that a reader could pick between. Any rater correction, even a fix to one weak test, requires re-running every scenario of the set, the costliest possible repair, and it gives a cheap re-rating no place to land; its weight depends on how often the rater calibration gate lets a rater version change.

A comparison set is defined by the seed tag, one version of each prompt per phase, the operator definition, and the rater definition; a new rater version re-rates the existing runs into a new set over the same runs. The host CLI version is not part of the set: it stays recorded in each manifest, as today, auto-update is left as it is, and the analysis reports which host versions a set's runs span beside its results. No pinning mechanism or pre-flight check is needed and runs always use the host as users actually receive it, while the factors the draft itself names as result-changing (operator, rater) are still held fixed within a set. A campaign that spans several days can mix host versions inside one set, so a margin between two scenarios may partly reflect a host change one of them happened to run under, against the attribution rule; the record only lets a reader see the mixing after the fact, not exclude it.

A comparison set is defined by the seed tag, one version of each prompt per phase, the operator definition, and the rater definition, with the rater bound to the campaign (runs are rated once, a new rater version only with a fresh set of runs). The host CLI version is recorded in each manifest only, not part of the set and not pinned, with the span of host versions reported beside the set's results. The set is the simplest operational unit, one campaign under one operator and one rater, with no host-control machinery and no question of which of two ratings of a run counts. It combines the uncontrolled host drift inside a set with the full re-run cost of every rater correction, so it carries both the attribution risk of an unpinned host and the highest repair cost of the rater axis.

A comparison set is defined by the seed tag, one version of each prompt per phase, the operator definition, the rater definition, and the host CLI version, but the host version is not pinned: auto-update is left on, and the analysis groups runs by the host version their manifests record, so a host update mid-campaign splits the runs into two sets. A new rater version re-rates existing runs into a new set over the same runs. No result ever mixes host versions, as with pinning, yet the harness needs no control over the host's installation, only the manifest field it already writes. An update arriving mid-campaign leaves a partial set that may never complete and forces the remaining scenarios, and possibly the finished ones, to be run again under the new version, so the timing of the host's release schedule decides how much of a campaign is wasted; what "complete" means for such a split set depends on the roster question.

A comparison set is defined by the seed tag, one version of each prompt per phase, the operator definition, the rater definition, and the recorded host CLI version, with the host unpinned (an update splits the runs into a new set by their recorded version) and the rater bound to the campaign (runs rated once, a new rater version only with fresh runs). Every version a set depends on is held fixed without any host-control machinery, and each set remains a single campaign rated once, so there is never a choice between ratings or a mixed host inside a set. Both kinds of change force fresh runs, a host update arriving on its own schedule and any rater correction alike, so it is the costliest option to keep current and the likeliest to leave sets incomplete.

open-question.question: Nothing lists which scenarios a comparison set must contain, so "complete" is undefined and the strongest manual strategy can be left out while the radar claims to compare against it. Does a comparison set declare a roster of scenarios that must all be rated before it counts as complete, and what must the roster hold?
open-question.alternative: A comparison set declares no roster. "Complete" is defined as every scenario that has at least one run in the set having both phases of each of its runs rated. The radar's claim about "the strongest manual configuration" is narrowed to "the best manual configuration this set ran", and the line under the chart already names the scenario each curve comes from. Adds no new input file and no planning step. The draft's completeness condition and its radar wording become exact about what they promise, and the set stays free to run whatever the maintainer can afford. Omission is still possible. A set can leave out the strongest manual configuration, or every multi-prompt control, and still count as complete, so it is the reader who has to notice from the scenario ids that a stronger manual pair was never run. A set's coverage depends on what happened to be run, not on a rule.

Each comparison set has a roster file in the benchmark's inputs area that lists scenario ids. It is declared before the set's first scored run and not changed during the set. The set is complete once every listed scenario has its runs rated in both phases, and the README page draws only from roster scenarios. No rule constrains what the roster lists. "Complete" gets an exact, pre-declared meaning, and once a set has started it cannot pick its comparison after seeing the scores. All this costs is one short file per set. Nothing stops the roster itself from leaving out the strongest manual configuration, so the radar's fairness claim still rests on the maintainer's judgment at declaration time. How a roster change relates to set identity depends on how the comparison set is defined.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run and fixed for the set, as a file in the inputs area. It must hold at least the following: cairn yolo and cairn assess for the set's Cairn version under the reference strategy models_strategy_1; the multi-prompt mirror of that cairn yolo scenario; and manual_prompt under the single pair named by a stated rule, namely the most capable model the set's pinned host version offers at that model's highest effort level. Further scenarios may be listed on top of this minimum. The radar's claim to compare against the strongest manual configuration is guaranteed by construction at the cost of one manual scenario, and every primary delivery appears in every set. The headline comparison can therefore never be read against a deliberately weak baseline. "Strongest" is assumed, not measured. Highest effort on the top model is not guaranteed to score best on this project, and "most capable" still needs a stated reading when the host offers models that trade one strength for another. Each run multiplies the cost of every mandatory scenario, depending on how many runs a set requires per scenario.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run and fixed for the set. It must hold at least the following: cairn yolo and cairn assess under models_strategy_1; the multi-prompt mirror of that cairn yolo scenario; and manual_prompt under every model the set's pinned host version offers, each at its highest effort level. The strongest manual configuration is then whichever of these scores highest, not one named in advance. The strongest manual configuration is found by measurement instead of being assumed, which closes the gap a rule-named pair leaves. It also gives the manual family several configurations, as Cairn has, so a best-of selection is not lopsided between families. Several manual scenarios per set multiply the cost of every set, run counts included. Choosing the best of several manual configurations brings in the best-of-noise selection effect that the radar curve rule has to account for, so how well this option works depends on how each family's curve is selected.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run and fixed for the set, as a matrix rather than a list. It names a set of single-pair model strategies (each model the pinned host offers, at its highest effort) plus Cairn's reference strategy. Every primary delivery runs under every single-pair strategy: manual_prompt, the multi-prompt mirror of each cairn yolo scenario, cairn yolo, and cairn assess. The two cairn deliveries also run under models_strategy_1. The set is complete only when every cell is rated. Every delivery is compared with every other under identical model pairs, so the attribution rule that "two scenarios sharing a strategy isolate the delivery" holds across the whole page. Every family also has the same configurations, which removes the selection asymmetry between Cairn and manual at its source. This is the most expensive roster by far, since cost grows with deliveries times strategies times runs. Most of the cells run Cairn under a single pair it is not meant to be used with, so most of the spend measures configurations that do not reflect Cairn as it is used.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run with the same mandatory minimum as the rule-named option. That minimum is cairn yolo and cairn assess under models_strategy_1, the multi-prompt mirror of that yolo scenario, and manual_prompt under the most capable host model at its highest effort. Scenarios may be added to the roster while the set is in progress, but none is ever removed, and the set is complete once every scenario on the final roster is rated. The baseline guarantee holds, and a stronger manual pair or a new Cairn release that turns up mid-campaign can still join the set without starting a new one, which matters for a campaign that spans several days. Additions made after scores are visible bring back post-hoc selection. A configuration can be added because an early result looked promising, which biases best-of curve selection, and a set whose roster keeps growing may never count as complete. Whether a mid-set addition is allowed at all depends on how the comparison set is defined.

open-question.question: The published trend follows per-scenario aggregates across comparison sets and plugin commits, so a change to the inputs and a change to the plugin are mixed in one line, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions. How does the trend continue when a shared input changes?
open-question.alternative: The trend is kept within one comparison set. When a shared input changes, every plugin commit already on the trend is re-run under the new set, so every point on the published line shares the same seed, prompts, operator, and every other shared input, and a step between two points can only come from the plugin. The previous set's trend is kept as an archived record and is never joined to the new one. This is the gaps report's proposed fix (gap 12). Every difference along the line comes from the plugin commit alone, which fully meets the draft's attribution rule (":7", ":11"), and the trend always shows the full release history under the current inputs, the best ones the benchmark has. Each input change costs a full chain and a rater run for every release on the trend, times the runs each scenario needs, and that cost keeps growing as releases accumulate. Old commits may no longer run under a newer host CLI or model, and then they drop off the line anyway. How often this cost comes due depends on which versions define a comparison set, which a sibling question owns; a set keyed to an auto-updating CLI would trigger it often. Which scenarios each re-run covers depends on the roster, which another sibling owns.

When a shared input changes, a fixed number of the most recent releases (stated in the draft, for example the last two or three) is re-run under the new set. A new trend segment starts at the oldest re-run release. Older points stay in the previous segment, drawn as a separate line with the input change marked at the break, and no line ever crosses a segment boundary. Each segment stays fully attributable to the plugin, the re-run cost of each input change is bounded no matter how many releases exist, and the recent history most relevant to current development carries over into the new segment. The long-range trend falls into segments that cannot be compared with each other, so the trend cannot show cumulative progress beyond the window. The window size is a judgment call the draft has to defend. The cost per input change is still several releases' worth of runs, and it comes due as often as the comparison-set definition, owned by a sibling, starts a new set.

Nothing is re-run when a shared input changes. The trend restarts as a new segment under the new comparison set and grows only as later commits are benchmarked under it. Each segment is drawn on its own, with the input change that opened it labeled at the boundary, and no line crosses from one segment to the next. The release gate already runs the previous release under the candidate's inputs, so a new segment starts with at least that pair. It needs no runs beyond those the release gate and the development loop already make, and every segment still obeys the attribution rule, because a line never joins points taken under different inputs. Each input change throws away the trend's history. If inputs change about as often as releases ship, segments stay two or three points long and the trend says little more than the release-gate comparison. How often that happens depends on the comparison-set definition a sibling owns.

When a shared input changes, one anchor release (the latest on the trend) is re-run under the new set. The new segment is then shifted by the anchor's score difference between the old and new sets, so the published trend stays one continuous line. The splice point and the estimated input effect are stated on the line. It keeps one continuous long-range trend for the cost of a single release's re-run per input change, and unlike an unmarked join it measures the input effect and reports it instead of folding it silently into the plugin's line. The splice assumes an input change shifts every commit's score by the same amount, which a new prompt, rater, or operator has no reason to do. Errors from successive splices add up along the line, and the anchor's shift is itself a difference of two noisy scores, as reliable as the runs per scenario a sibling question sets. The line therefore still mixes input and plugin effects, only less visibly, which goes against the attribution rule.

The trend gets its own comparison set whose shared inputs are pinned and never revised. Every release is benchmarked under that frozen set for the trend, alongside whatever newer set drives the README page's ranking and radar. Input revisions go only into the newer sets. A segment break happens only when a frozen input can no longer be run at all, for example a retired model. Every point on the trend shares identical inputs for as long as they stay runnable, with no back-catalogue re-runs, so the line is both continuous and fully attributable to the plugin. Every release pays for a second campaign on the frozen set, and the trend keeps measuring against inputs the benchmark has already found worth fixing (a corrected prompt, a calibrated rater), so it can disagree with the current page. Model retirement and host CLI updates force breaks anyway. Whether the CLI can be pinned at all depends on the comparison-set definition a sibling owns.

The trend stays as the draft has it: per-scenario aggregates followed across comparison sets and plugin commits as one line. Each input change is marked on the line with what changed, and the draft states that the trend is a descriptive history that attributes nothing, carving it out of the attribution rule. It costs no runs and no new machinery, and it keeps the longest unbroken view of how the scores moved over the benchmark's life. A step at an input change cannot be split between plugin and inputs. Cairn's changelog links to the trend for each release, which invites exactly the attribution the carve-out disclaims, and the draft's own statement that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions then has a published exception.

No trend across comparison sets or plugin commits is published. The README page keeps the current set's ranking and radar. Each release's changelog entry links instead to that release's gate comparison, the candidate against the previous release under the same inputs and model strategy. The "Published trend" use is removed from the draft, or deferred as a convention with the reason stated. It removes the confound entirely without adding cost, since the release gate already produces a within-set comparison for every release, which is the attributable form of what a trend would show. The benchmark loses any long-range view of Cairn's progress across releases, so a reader or a grant reviewer can see only pairwise steps and the current standing, not whether the plugin has improved over time.

open-question.question: Phase 2 starts as soon as the parent's Run: commit exists, which implies runs in parallel, yet every run's pre-flight requires the benchmark checkout to be on a clean main and every run commits to it. Are runs sequential, or how do concurrent runs share the benchmark checkout?
open-question.alternative: Runs are strictly sequential: at most one run of the procedure is in progress at a time on the one benchmark checkout, enforced by the harness (a run refuses to start while another holds the run lock) rather than by convention. The one-run procedure keeps its clean-main pre-flight, its live reads of the inputs area, and its own Run: commit unchanged. "As soon as the parent's Run: commit exists" is reworded as a queue-ordering rule (a phase-2 run may be queued once its parent's Run: commit exists, with no wait on any rating), not as parallelism. Concurrency is not designed now; adding it later is a harness change versioned like any other. Removes the contradiction with no new machinery: pre-flight, input reads, snapshot, manifest, and commit stay exactly as drafted, main has one writer by construction, no sibling clone exists on disk while a run executes, and each run's wall-clock duration is measured on an otherwise idle machine and account, so the time column compares across runs. A comparison set's wall-clock becomes the sum of every run of every scenario in both phases, each a multi-invocation chain, so a set spans days or longer; that lengthens the window in which the host CLI or the model can change mid-set, which matters to the degree the comparison-set definition does not pin those versions.

Runs execute concurrently, each in its own clone as drafted, against the one shared benchmark checkout. The pre-flight drops "on main and clean" as a precondition held for the run's duration: it takes a short exclusive lock on the checkout, asserts main is clean at that moment, records main's commit in the manifest, and the run then reads every input (prompt, hidden-requirement entries, operator definition, delivery, strategy) from that recorded commit through git objects rather than from the live working tree. Steps 7 to 10 (snapshot, manifest, index regeneration, Run: commit) run under the same lock, one run at a time, on the shared checkout's main. The smallest change that permits parallelism on one machine: one checkout, one lock file, main stays linear with one Run: commit per run, and pinning inputs to the pre-flight commit keeps each run's input versions exact even as other runs' commits move main underneath it. The shared working tree changes under running runs, so every input read must go through the recorded commit and a single live read is a silent version leak; a run that dies holding the lock blocks every other run's recording until it is cleared; concurrent runs share one account's usage window and one machine, so per-run wall-clock reflects load and must be read with the concurrency level recorded; and sibling clones sit side by side on disk, which is safe only as far as the filesystem-confinement decision makes it.

Runs execute concurrently, and each run's harness side works in its own git worktree of the benchmark repository, detached at main's tip when the run starts. The pre-flight asserts that this worktree is clean, every input is read from it, and steps 7 to 9 write the snapshot and manifest there and commit Run: in the worktree. Landing is serialised behind a lock: under it the Run: commit is rebased onto current main (its paths, runs/<id>/ and results/<id>/, are disjoint from every other run's), the index page is regenerated on the result, and main is fast-forwarded to it; the worktree is then removed with the clone. The pre-flight's "clean checkout" check keeps its full meaning per run and every input is read from a private, fixed tree with no special read path, while main stays linear and the lock is held only for the brief landing, so parallelism costs no change to how a run reads or writes its own record. More harness machinery than either simpler option (worktree creation and removal, a rebase step, regenerating the index on every landing, recovery of a worktree and lock left by a crashed run); the Run: commit order on main follows landing order, not start order; and the shared-account usage window, load-dependent wall-clock, and side-by-side clones carry over as in any concurrent option, the last safe only as far as the filesystem-confinement decision makes it.

Runs execute concurrently, possibly on several machines, and each run's harness side works in its own fresh clone of the benchmark repository's main rather than in a worktree of one local checkout. The pre-flight asserts that clone is clean and records its commit; inputs are read from it; the run commits Run: there and pushes to the canonical remote's main, which serves as the serialisation point: on a non-fast-forward rejection the run fetches, rebases its disjoint-path commit, regenerates the index page, and retries. No local lock exists, and phase 2's "the parent's Run: commit exists" is read on the canonical remote. The only option in which runs need not share one machine or one local checkout, so a set can be spread across machines or isolated environments (each run carrying its own benchmark clone), which is the shape a confined or remote execution environment naturally takes. Every landing is a network round trip that can lose a race and retry, the regenerated index page conflicts on every rebase and must be rebuilt each time, and a run that cannot push holds a finished record that exists nowhere else; whether multi-machine execution is wanted at all depends on the execution-environment and filesystem-confinement decisions, and runs on different machines also differ in the environment each records.

Runs execute concurrently and none of them writes to main: the one-run procedure ends at a record step that writes the snapshot source, manifest, and invocation outputs to a per-run record ref (for example record/<id>) on the canonical repository, never cloned by a run since run clones are single-branch, and the pre-flight's clean-main assertion is replaced by recording the main commit the run read its inputs from. A separate collector, the only writer of main and always sequential, imports each finished record into runs/<id>/ and results/<id>/, regenerates the index, and commits Run: <id>. Phase 2 may start as soon as the parent's run branch and record ref exist, before the collector has committed it. Rejects the premise that each run commits to main: main gets exactly one writer whatever the concurrency, runs never contend for anything local, and phase 2 no longer waits even on the parent's Run: commit, so the pipeline runs at full parallelism with no lock in the run procedure at all. Adds a stage and a ref namespace the draft does not have: the parent check moves from a manifest on main to one on a record ref, a record that is pushed but not yet collected is invisible on main and on the Pages index, and the collector becomes one more harness component whose failures leave finished runs unrecorded; it also inherits the shared-account usage window and load-dependent wall-clock of every concurrent option.

open-question.question: Each hidden requirement's evidence must settle the question once asked while the prompt alone gives no reason to ask, and nothing has tested this: prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" may already invite the topic question, and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" sits close to the export convention. What procedure and acceptance rule calibrate each prompt's hidden requirement before scored runs?
open-question.alternative: A pre-run pilot, the design-gaps report's fix taken as written. For each prompt the draft states a pilot: the bare manual_prompt delivery is run a small fixed number of times (five, say) with the operator as defined, hidden knowledge included, under the comparison set's strongest manual model pair. Prompt 2's pilot runs start from the pilot's own phase-1 runs. The real rater scores the hidden check line. The acceptance rule is one band on the met rate: a requirement met in almost every run has evidence that is too strong, or a prompt that invites the question; one met in no run has evidence that is too faint; a rate between the two passes. A failure is fixed by revising the seed evidence (a seed bump) or the prompt and running the pilot again. Pilot runs belong to no comparison set and are never scored. It is the cheapest procedure that tests anything empirically, and it reuses the delivery, operator, and rater the draft already defines with no pilot-only machinery. The met rate mixes runs that met the requirement because they asked and were told with runs that inferred it unasked. A high rate could mean a model that asks well, not evidence that is too strong, so the band cannot tell which half of the calibration rule failed. A five-run band is also too coarse to separate a 20% rate from a 60% one.

A pre-run pilot with two arms per prompt, one for each half of the calibration rule, each run a small fixed number of times under the strongest manual model pair. The unasked arm runs manual_prompt with the operator's hidden knowledge withheld, so every question gets a reply that discloses nothing; it measures whether the prompt and seed lead to the requirement with no disclosure. Its acceptance rule is a met-rate ceiling. The asked arm gives a model the seed tree and the prompt plus one fixed bearing question written by the maintainer (what the questions should be about; where a written set should live), with no operator, and checks whether its answer, grounded in the evidence alone, is the hidden requirement. Its acceptance rule is a hit-rate floor. A requirement passes only when both arms pass. A failed ceiling is fixed by weakening the evidence or the prompt's invitation, and a failed floor by strengthening the evidence, each as a seed bump or prompt revision followed by another pilot. Pilot runs are never scored. Each half of the stated rule (no reason to ask from the prompt alone; one clearly best answer once asked) gets its own measurement and threshold, so a failure says whether to weaken or strengthen the evidence. The asked arm also checks the grounding the YOLO chain depends on when it accepts its own recommendation without the operator. It adds two pilot-only harness modes, an operator with its hidden knowledge stripped and a direct probe call, that no scored delivery uses. The asked arm's result depends on how the maintainer words the bearing question, which assumes the very question a run is supposed to surface. Its operator-withheld arm depends on how the sibling bearing-question test defines a disclosure-triggering question.

A pre-run pilot of every scenario in the planned roster, manual and Cairn deliveries alike, each run a few times per prompt with the operator as defined and rated by the real rater. The acceptance rule asks whether the hidden axis discriminates: a requirement passes when its met rate is neither at the ceiling nor at the floor across all scenarios together. When every scenario meets it, the evidence is too strong; when none does, too faint. A failure is fixed by revising the evidence or the prompt and running the pilot again. Pilot runs are excluded from every comparison set. It tests the axis for what it is meant to do, separating deliveries, under the exact conditions the scored runs will have, including Cairn's review and recommendation path, which a manual-only pilot never exercises. It costs about as much as a small comparison set. Tuning the evidence until the scenarios spread also tunes it against the deliveries being compared, which invites calibrating toward the Cairn margin the benchmark exists to test. Its scope depends on the roster the sibling scenario-roster question defines.

No pilot runs. The draft states an authoring checklist that each hidden requirement and its evidence must pass before the requirement is used. The evidence names neither the requirement nor its key word. The requirement is no convention of the project's category and appears on no implied-requirement or left-open list. The prompt contains no phrase that points at the bearing question (prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" are reviewed against this). The answer follows from the evidence only once the question is asked. The maintainer and one independent reader both judge each item, and the acceptance rule is that every item passes for both readers. A failure is fixed by rewording the evidence or the prompt before the inputs are used. It costs no runs and can be settled entirely in the draft, and it catches the two concerns the question names (the prompt's own invitation, and prompt 2's closeness to an export convention) as reviewable wording problems. It replaces the test the gap says is missing with the same kind of judgment that produced the untested evidence. Whether a model makes the zoo-to-animals inference unasked, or exports a set by habit, is empirical, and a reader's verdict on it can be wrong in either direction without anything showing it.

No separate pilot before scored runs. Calibration is checked once, after the first comparison set has been rated, by reading the operator records and ratings already kept. For each prompt the audit counts the runs that met the hidden requirement with no bearing question in the operator record (inferred unasked) and the runs that failed it although the statement was disclosed or the evidence was present. The acceptance rule is a ceiling on the first count and a ceiling on the second, stated in the draft. Until the audit passes, that set's hidden-axis scores are published marked provisional. A failure revises the evidence or the prompt for the next set, as a seed bump or prompt revision. It spends nothing beyond the scored runs, and it calibrates on the full run count and every delivery rather than a handful of pilot runs, so the rates it reads are less noisy than any affordable pilot's. The first set's hidden axis is spent on evidence nobody had tested and is published before calibration is known. The audit also turns the run record into a pass-fail judgment, which the draft has so far kept out of measurement, and it depends on how the sibling bearing-question test decides that a recorded question bore on the requirement.

No pre-run gate. Instead every comparison set carries one control: manual_prompt under the strongest manual model pair, run with the operator's hidden knowledge withheld. Its hidden-requirement met rate is reported beside the hidden axis as the floor that inference alone reaches, so a reader can see how much of each scenario's hidden score asking could have added. The requirement is kept whatever the control shows. The acceptance rule is disclosure only, with no threshold that blocks scored runs, and a revision stays the maintainer's call between sets. Calibration is measured in every set under that set's own models and host version, so the measurement stays current as models learn to infer more, and it never blocks a set or tunes the evidence toward a result. A requirement whose evidence is too strong or too faint keeps being scored, with the problem only disclosed beside it. Each set pays for an extra scenario. Whether the control belongs in a set depends on the roster the sibling scenario-roster question defines.

The empirical calibration requirement is dropped. The draft states no pilot procedure and no acceptance rule. It keeps the calibration bullet as an authoring intent only and says plainly that the evidence has not been tested: prompt 1's wording may invite the topic question, and prompt 2's request sits close to an export convention. The hidden axis is read with that limitation. It costs nothing and adds no procedure to a benchmark that has not been implemented yet, and it is honest about what the design does and does not guarantee. The axis may then measure whether a model read README.md, which the draft itself rules out as a valid hidden requirement, and nothing would ever show whether it does. The milestone goal names the hidden-requirement pilot as a gap to resolve by stated procedure, so this option rejects that gap and must give its reason in the draft.

open-question.question: The animal reading line scores the count of animal questions out of ten, which is undefined for an artifact that holds more than ten questions or draws ten per game. How is that line scored for such an artifact?
open-question.alternative: The items of the animal reading line become every question a game of the artifact can ask, read from its source (a question no game can reach, such as an eleventh entry of a fixed-order list that only ever asks ten, is not an item), and the score is the animal items over the items, scaled to 100, the general reading-line rule of "The rater" applied as written. For an artifact of exactly ten questions this gives the same number as the current count out of ten, so the hidden-axis example (ten animal questions score 100, seven score 70) stands, and the check line in "Prompt 1: the game" is reworded from "the ten questions" and "out of ten" to every question a game can ask. Deterministic and repeatable, since it reads the bank rather than one random draw, and it equals the expected share of animal questions in a game drawn uniformly, so it reads what a room would see on average while reusing the rule every reading line already follows rather than adding a special case. A large bank (fifty or two hundred questions) has to be read whole, raising the rater's reading cost and the room for a misread item, deciding which entries a game can reach is a reading of draw logic the rater must get right, and a bank with a few stray non-animal questions scores close to 100 although some games the host runs will show them.

The items are every question a game of the artifact can ask, read from its source, and the score is that of the worst game the artifact could put on screen: ten minus the number of non-animal items (floored at zero), over ten, scaled to 100. An artifact of exactly ten questions scores as today; a bank of fifty with three non-animal questions scores 70, because one game may draw all three. The check line in "Prompt 1: the game" is reworded to state this rule. Reads the requirement as it is written, every question about an animal, against any game the host might run on the evening rather than an average one, and stays deterministic and equal to the current count out of ten for a ten-question artifact. Harsh on large banks, which reach zero after ten stray questions however many animal questions surround them, so it penalises an artifact for holding more questions than the prompt asked for, and it shares the whole-bank reading cost and reachability judgment of reading every askable question.

The line keeps its wording and its count out of ten: the rater plays one game through to the standings and reads the ten questions that game asks, whatever the artifact holds or how it draws them, and the score is the animal count out of ten. Questions the game did not ask are not read. Needs no change to the line or to the hidden-axis example, keeps the reading to ten items whatever the bank's size, and scores exactly what a room sees in a game. For an artifact that draws ten at random, two ratings of the same artifact can read different questions and get different numbers, against the scoring section's claim that a second rating gets the same number, and non-animal questions outside the drawn ten go unseen, so the score depends on the draw rather than on the artifact.

The line keeps its count out of ten and the rater reads the ten questions one played game asks, but the harness makes the draw repeatable by fixing the browser's random source (a seeded replacement for its random-number functions, installed before the artifact loads) whenever the rater plays the game for this line, so every rating of one artifact plays the same game. The rating guideline and the check line in "Prompt 1: the game" state the pinned draw. Keeps the line's wording, its ten-item reading, and the score of exactly what a room sees, while restoring the repeatability an unpinned played game loses. The ten read are an arbitrary sample fixed by the harness's seed, so a bank whose stray questions fall outside the pinned draw scores 100 by chance and changing the seed can change the score; it adds a harness mechanism of its own, and an artifact that draws through a source the harness does not pin, or by time, escapes it.

open-question.question: "About an animal" has borderline items, such as the zoo's visitor count or how many animals live at the zoo, while a reading line promises one defensible answer per item. Does the hidden-requirement entry state a classification rule for borderline items?
open-question.alternative: The prompt 1 hidden-requirement entry states a classification rule. A question is about an animal when the number it asks for counts animals or measures an animal or an animal kind: its body, lifespan, diet, speed, offspring, or behaviour. A question about anything else fails, the zoo's own operations included (visitors, staff, ticket prices, opening years). The entry gives the gap's two items as worked verdicts: how many animals live at Riverside Zoo passes and the zoo's visitor count fails. The reading-line definition and the requirement's wording stay as they are. It settles both cited borderline items and the obvious variants of them with one test the rater can apply and a reader can check, so the promise of one defensible answer per item holds without changing what the stakeholder is said to want. The line between counting animals and describing the zoo stays a judgment at its edges, for example the number of keepers per elephant or the size of the penguin enclosure. Whether two ratings agree on those edges is measured only where the rater-calibration and repeat-rating questions put a check.

The entry states a stricter rule. A question passes only when its answer is a fact about an animal kind (a species or a group such as birds) that holds independently of any particular place or institution. A count or measure tied to Riverside Zoo or any other zoo fails, including how many animals live at the zoo, and so does the visitor count. The entry gives both items as worked fail verdicts. The requirement's wording stays as it is. It is the sharpest rule of the set: membership turns on whether the answer is a general fact of nature, which also screens out questions about the fictional zoo whose numbers have no checkable source. It is narrower than the stakeholder's evident wish, a zoo members' evening where a question about the zoo's own animals would be welcome. An artifact that read the evidence well can then lose points on questions a person would call animal questions, which makes the hidden axis partly a test of guessing the rule.

The hidden requirement itself is restated from "every question is about an animal" to "every question is about animals or the zoo", with a rule saying a question passes when the number it asks for concerns an animal, an animal kind, or Riverside Zoo and its running. Both cited items pass. The entry gives them as worked verdicts, and a question about neither (a city's population, a historical date unrelated to the zoo) fails. It removes the cited borderline by moving the class to the boundary the seed's evidence (the zoo's members' evening) actually supports, so an artifact is not penalised for a zoo question the stakeholder would accept. It changes the hidden requirement rather than clarifying it. That loosens what the evidence must make clearly best, which the hidden-requirement pilot question's calibration then has to cover, and it moves the borderline to a new edge, for example questions about the zoo's town or about conservation in general.

The entry states a near-mechanical rule: a question passes when its text names an animal, an animal kind, or animals as a group, whatever the number it asks for. How many animals live at Riverside Zoo passes, and the zoo's visitor count fails unless its wording names an animal. The entry gives both as worked verdicts. Two raters, or a rater and a reader, all but always reach the same verdict, because the check reads the question's words rather than weighing its topic. It scores wording rather than topic, so a question such as "how many people queued to see the pandas" passes while being about visitors. That lets an artifact that only sprinkled animal words score as if it met the requirement.

The entry states no class rule of its own. The reading-line definition in the rater section gains one general rule for every reading line: an item whose class membership the rater cannot settle from the line's wording is recorded as doubtful with its reason and scored as failing. The two cited items are left to that rule. One sentence covers this line and any future reading line, and the doubt is made visible in the recorded verdicts instead of hidden in a silent call either way. Whether an item is doubtful is itself a judgment, so the promise of one defensible answer moves rather than holds. Failing every doubtful item also biases the line against artifacts whose questions lean on the zoo, which the stakeholder may well have welcomed.

No classification rule is added, either in the entry or in the reading-line definition. The draft records the gap as rejected, giving as its reason that every item and verdict is recorded as the line's evidence for a reader to check, and that borderline items are expected to be few among ten built-in questions. The requirement and the reading-line promise stay worded as they are. It adds nothing to the inputs and keeps the hidden requirement in the stakeholder's own plain words, relying on evidence the design already records. The promise of one defensible answer per item stays unmet for exactly the items the gap names. A borderline question can then score differently between two ratings, and the rater's model decides it unseen, which is the noise the axes section says no line carries.

open-question.question: The benchmark's main branch is public, so the hidden requirements, the operator records, and every artifact are public and future models will train on them, wearing down the no-canned-solution requirement over time. How does the benchmark limit or account for its inputs and results leaking into training data?
open-question.alternative: Everything stays public as the draft has it now: inputs, operator records, invocation outputs, run branches, snapshots, and ratings. Nothing is marked for exclusion, nothing is flagged, and nothing is rotated. The draft instead states leakage as a known limitation: a comparison set runs every scenario on the same models, so whatever a model has absorbed reaches every scenario of the set, and the hidden axis is expected to lose discriminating power as the inputs age. It costs nothing and keeps the design fully open and reproducible. Every artifact stays playable by URL, every input stays inspectable, and the limitation is stated honestly in the text rather than half-solved. The erosion does not hit all scenarios equally. A model that has seen "every question is about an animal" next to the zoo README can meet the hidden requirement without asking. That helps the manual deliveries most, because asking the operator is their only other route, so Cairn's measured hidden-axis gain shrinks silently and nothing tells a reader when it happened. The Closest Wins hidden requirements are also already stated in the public Cairn repository's draft, so the clock is already running.

Everything stays public. Every published file the benchmark writes (the inputs area, the records, the evaluation area, the README page, and the project section of the draft) carries one fixed benchmark canary string asking training pipelines to exclude it, following the BIG-bench convention. The seed is left unmarked so that no run sees the canary. There is no contamination accounting and no rotation. It is the cheapest real limiting measure and an established convention. Cooperating trainers can drop the content, and anyone can probe a model for the canary to test whether it trained on the benchmark, with no change to openness, publishing, or the run procedure. Exclusion depends on trainers honouring the string, and nothing stops copies that strip it. The draft and the gaps report are already public without it. The snapshots carry the seed README and the questions together, so an unmarked mirror of an artifact leaks the pairing anyway. The benchmark still has no way to tell a reader whether a given comparison set was run on a contaminated model.

Everything stays public with the canary string as in canary marking. In addition, each shared input records the date it was first published, the manifest or comparison-set definition records each model's vendor-stated training cutoff, and the analysis flags every comparison set where any model's cutoff falls after its inputs' first publication. The README page shows that flag beside the ranking table and the radar. Inputs are never rotated. It turns a silent erosion into a visible, dated property of each result. A reader can tell an uncontaminated comparison from a possibly contaminated one, and openness, playable artifacts, and trend continuity stay intact. Vendor cutoffs are approximate and sometimes unpublished, and a cutoff after publication shows only exposure, not use, so the flag is coarse in both directions. It records the damage without restoring discriminating power: once the frontier models postdate the inputs, every new set is flagged and the hidden axis means less with each one. How the flag interacts with set identity depends on which versions define a comparison set.

Everything stays public with the canary and the contamination flag as above.
