A flagged set, or inputs older than a stated age where no cutoff is published, triggers a rotation before the next headline comparison set. The rotation brings new hidden requirements with new seed evidence, and the prompts or the whole project change when the leak reaches the project's own rules. Only then is the old project retired, still public. It is the only fully open option that keeps the hidden axis meaningful indefinitely. Every retired input stays public and reproducible, while the scored inputs are always ones no model could have trained on. Every rotation is a seed and prompt bump that starts a new comparison set and breaks the trend's continuity. Each new hidden requirement needs its own calibration before scored runs, and authoring a project that meets every project requirement is recurring work. Its cost depends on how the trend continues across input changes and on what the hidden-requirement pilot procedure costs.

The statements the scoring rests on move to a separate private repository the harness reads. These are the hidden-requirement entries, the rating checklist's hidden lines, the operator definition, and the operator records and invocation outputs that quote its disclosures. The public main keeps the harness, the published snapshots, manifests stripped of operator content, the ratings without hidden-line evidence, and the aggregates. The draft in the Cairn repository describes the hidden requirement abstractly and stops naming it, and the current Closest Wins hidden requirements are replaced because they are already public. It removes the one thing whose leak most directly defeats the benchmark, the written statement of each hidden requirement and its check. It does that while keeping artifacts playable and most of the design inspectable. The published snapshots still leak the pairing. Each snapshot is the whole tree, seed README included, and every artifact that met the requirement shows the answer, so a model trained on enough snapshots can learn it without ever seeing the statement. External readers can no longer audit how the hidden axis was scored, and the benchmark now depends on a private repository the "one canonical repository" layout does not have.

The benchmark repository, its run branches, and its snapshots are private, and GitHub Pages publishes no artifacts. The only public output is the ranking table, the radar, and the trend, on a public page or in Cairn's changelog. The Cairn draft names no hidden requirement, and Closest Wins' current hidden requirements are replaced because the draft has already published them. It is the strongest limit available. Nothing scrapeable carries the inputs, the artifacts, or the records, so the no-canned-solution requirement and the hidden axis wear down only through deliberate disclosure. It gives up what the README page is built on: artifacts a reader can open and compare side by side as proof, and a record anyone can audit or re-run. The published scores become claims a reader must take on trust, which weakens them as evidence of whether Cairn helps, the benchmark's stated purpose.

The benchmark keeps two input sets. A public development set (the current project, prompts, and hidden requirements, fully published as now, artifacts included) serves the fast loop, ablations, and candidate commits. A private held-out set (its own prompts or hidden requirements, with its artifacts and records unpublished while live) is the only input behind the README page's ranking table and radar. When the held-out set is retired it is published in full and replaced by a fresh one. It keeps development fully open and reproducible while the headline comparison runs on inputs no model can have trained on, and retiring the held-out set publishes it eventually, so nothing stays secret for good. Every held-out set needs its own authoring and calibration, which doubles the input work. Headline artifacts are not playable and the headline cannot be audited externally while the set is live. Development results and headline results are on different inputs, so the fast loop no longer predicts the page directly. Each replacement is an input change whose trend continuity depends on how the trend continues across input changes.

open-question.question: Each prompt's checklist is derived from the draft's project section, which no version pins, and nothing freezes the checklist and hidden requirements before a comparison set's first scored run. Are the checklist and hidden-requirement entries frozen before the first scored run of a set, and how?
open-question.alternative: Nothing is pinned. Each rating derives the checklist from the project section as it stands when the rating runs, and the hidden-requirement entries stay editable at any point. The manifest and rating files record no version of either, and the analysis groups runs only by the inputs it already records (seed tag, prompt blobs). Adds no input, field, or harness check, and a defect found in a checklist line or a hidden entry can be fixed the moment someone sees it. Two ratings in one comparison set can be scored against different checklists with no record of it. Nothing stops a checklist line or hidden check from being reworded after results are seen. This breaks the draft's own rule that every shared input is recorded by content and that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions.

The project section the checklist is derived from (per prompt, together with every earlier prompt's section) is recorded by blob hash in each manifest and rating file, and so is each hidden-requirement entry. The checklist itself stays unmaterialized and is re-derived from the pinned section at each rating. There is no gate: an edit is a new version that the analysis groups by. Uses the draft's own versioning idiom (content hashes in the manifest) and the smallest change to the design: no new checklist file and no harness refusal. Pinning the source does not pin the derived lines. A rating agent turning prose into lines can split, merge, or reword them differently on each rating, so the line ids the lost-since-parent count depends on are not stable. Edits after results are seen are recorded but not prevented.

The checklist is materialized as one committed file per prompt in the inputs area, its lines carrying their ids, axes, and kinds. That file and each hidden-requirement entry are recorded by blob hash in every manifest and rating file. There is no gate before the first scored run. A changed hidden-requirement statement, which the operator reads, means fresh runs. A changed checklist or check line means the set's existing artifacts are re-rated against the new version, and the analysis never compares ratings made under different versions. Line ids and wording become a fixed artifact every rating reads, every rating is traceable to the exact lines it used, and a correction is cheap: a re-rating of artifacts that are already immutable snapshots. Nothing prevents tuning the lines or a hidden check after seeing which scenario they favour. The record makes such a change visible in the history but does not stop it, and re-rating under a convenient new version is easy. Whether these hashes become part of a comparison set's identity depends on how a comparison set is defined.

As in Record by content, the checklist is materialized per prompt in the inputs area, and it and each hidden-requirement entry are recorded by blob hash in every manifest. Both are treated as shared run inputs like the seed and the prompts, so any change to either starts a new comparison set with fresh runs of every scenario. There is still no gate before the first scored run. One uniform rule for every shared input: a change of any of them is a new set. A set never holds artifacts rated against two checklists, and no separate rating-version concept is needed for the checklist. A typo fix in one checklist line costs a full re-run of every scenario, which the immutable artifacts did not need. The first scored runs can still start before the inputs settle, so early sets are likely to be thrown away. This option depends on comparison-set identity including these hashes and on how superseded sets are shown.

The checklist is materialized per prompt in the inputs area and committed with the hidden-requirement entries before a set's first scored run. Their blob hashes are fixed as the set's frozen versions. The harness refuses a scored run, and the rater refuses a rating, whose checklist or hidden entry differs from the frozen versions. Any later change to either starts a new comparison set with fresh runs of every scenario. Gives the strongest guarantee against post-hoc tuning, a pre-registration in effect. Every artifact in a set was produced and rated against inputs fixed before any result existed, and the harness enforces this rather than discipline. Combines the costliest correction (a full re-run for any fix) with a new harness check. The freeze is only as good as the inputs at freeze time, so it has to follow whatever calibration of hidden requirements and rater happens before scored runs. Like Record, new set, it depends on comparison-set identity and on how superseded sets are shown.

The checklist is materialized per prompt in the inputs area and committed with the hidden-requirement entries before a set's first scored run. Their blob hashes are fixed as frozen versions, and the harness refuses a scored run that does not match them. After the freeze, a changed hidden-requirement statement, which the operator reads, starts a new comparison set with fresh runs. A changed checklist line or hidden check line is issued as a new rating version that re-rates every artifact of the set. The earlier ratings and frozen version are kept, and the analysis never mixes versions. Pre-registers the first version before any result exists, so every later revision is visibly a revision. A correction to rating-side lines costs only a re-rating of the immutable artifacts, not a re-run. Uses two change paths (run-side and rating-side) where one rule would do, and the hidden-requirement entry is split across them. Revisions after results are seen remain possible, and they are visible but not prevented. Its rating-version path has to fit whatever acceptance rule a rater version must pass before it may rate a set.

open-question.question: The README shows only the latest complete comparison set, so a seed bump replaces a bad result on the landing page with no trace. Does the page keep superseded comparison sets linked with the reason each was superseded?

The operator's input is the prompt text as committed, which in phase 2 is prompt 2 alone, so a phase-2 question about the game's existing flow reaches a stakeholder who does not know the game they asked for in phase 1. Which prompts does the operator receive in phase n?
open-question.alternative: In phase n the operator receives prompt n alone, as the draft states now ("its input is always the prompt text as committed"), at every reactive turn and at the assess delivery's planned turn. It is told nothing of earlier prompts, and the general guideline gains no rule for questions about what an earlier phase built. The gap is rejected in the draft with its reason stated. Nothing in the operator's definition changes, and its input stays the one committed file every scenario shares, while everything the stakeholder asked for in phase 1 is already readable by the run itself in the `Prompt: 1` commit, so the operator holds no knowledge about the existing game that the run could not reach on its own. A phase-2 question about the game's existing flow reaches a stakeholder who does not know there is a game, so its reply is improvised. It may answer "I don't know what game you mean", which steers the run or betrays that it is not a person, and that improvisation varies with how each scenario words its question, so it is not identical across scenarios.

alternative.id: Current prompt only, with a deferral rule

open-question.alternative: In phase n the operator still receives prompt n alone, at every turn, and the general guideline gains one rule: a question about anything its input does not cover, the existing project and what was built before included, gets the guideline's taste deferral ("your call"), never a statement that it does not know. The draft states that a run learns the earlier request from its own tree and history, as the phase-2 pointer sentence already intends. It removes the incoherent reply at the cost of one sentence in the guideline, adds no input and no versioned text to the operator, and keeps every fact about phase 1 on the run's side, so the benchmark still measures whether the run itself reads its history. The stakeholder answers "your call" to a question that a real stakeholder could settle from their own first request, such as whether the editor must keep the six-step flow they asked for, so a run that asks the person rather than reading its history is told less than a person would have told it, which penalises asking in phase 2 relative to phase 1.

alternative.id: Prompts 1 to n, current hidden statements

open-question.alternative: In phase n the operator receives prompts 1 to n, taken byte-identical from the versioned prompt texts the manifest records, at every reactive turn and at the assess delivery's planned turn; the earlier prompts are marked as the stakeholder's earlier requests and prompt n as the current one. Its hidden knowledge stays phase n's statements only. The draft's sentence on the operator's input changes from "the prompt text as committed" to the prompts up to the current phase, and no versioning changes, because a revision of prompt 1 already invalidates both phases. The stakeholder knows everything it has asked for, as a real one making a second request does, so a phase-2 question about the existing game gets an answer grounded in what was actually asked, while each prompt's hidden measurement stays its own because only phase n's statements can be disclosed. The operator now knows phase-1 requirements and can state them in reply to a phase-2 question, so a run that asks instead of reading its own history gets prompt 1 restated for it, which narrows the very contrast phase 2 exists to show between a workflow that recorded its decisions and a run that did not; the earlier-request marking must also be worded so the operator never presents prompt 1 as a fresh demand.

alternative.id: Prompts 1 to n, all hidden statements

open-question.alternative: In phase n the operator receives prompts 1 to n, marked as earlier and current requests as above, at every turn, and its hidden knowledge holds the hidden statements of phases 1 to n, any of which it discloses under the same reactive rule; only phase n's statement is scored, as now. The draft drops "those of the current prompt only" from the hidden-knowledge layer. The operator is one consistent person across the phases: what it wanted at phase 1 it still wants at phase 2, so a phase-2 question that touches the first request's unstated expectation, such as what the host's own questions should be about, gets the same answer it would have got at phase 1. It breaks the rule that keeps each prompt's measurement its own: an earlier statement can now be disclosed in a phase whose rating does not score it, steering the phase-2 artifact by knowledge no phase-2 line checks, and a phase-2 disclosure of the phase-1 statement becomes one more thing a case-by-case reading must tell apart in the record.

alternative.id: Prompts 1 to n with the parent's operator record

open-question.alternative: In phase n the operator receives prompts 1 to n and, beside them, the operator record files of the parent run's earlier phases (its own earlier inputs, replies, and closing lines), at every turn; its hidden knowledge stays phase n's statements only, although those records carry any earlier statement it disclosed. The draft states that this part of the operator's input is per-run rather than shared. The stakeholder remembers not only what it asked for but what it told this very run before, so it can never contradict one of its own earlier answers, which is the full memory a real stakeholder brings to a second request. The operator's input then differs between scenarios and runs, against the draft's rule that it is a shared input identical for every scenario, and the gain is small because under the guideline its phase-1 replies are almost all deferrals or hidden-statement disclosures; the records also carry an earlier hidden statement into a phase that does not score it.

open-question.question: The ranking-table section opens by saying the table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches, while the radar text says the page states no claim the data does not. Does that sentence change to say the table shows whether Cairn beats them?
open-question.alternative: The opening sentence of "The ranking table" in ideas/benchmark_for_cairn.md stays as written ("The table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches as a family of configurations, not as one tuned winner"). No other sentence of the table or radar sections changes, and the draft records that the sentence was kept, with the reason, as the resolution of gap 18. It states plainly the result the benchmark was built to show. The radar's rule that the page states no claim the curves do not is about the generated page, not about this design prose, so the two need not conflict, and the draft is not edited at all. The draft would assert a result before any run exists. That contradicts its own refutable framing at the phase-2 expectation and in the radar text, and it is exactly the inconsistency the gaps report flags. It also reads as a benchmark designed to confirm its author's product, which weakens the "proof of whether Cairn helps" purpose stated in the general idea.

Only the opening sentence changes, from "shows that Cairn beats" to "shows whether Cairn beats the other approaches as a family of configurations, not as one tuned winner". The rest of the table section stays as written, including "The reading it exists to give is several Cairn rows … standing above the best manual row", and the radar section stays as written. It is the smallest edit that removes the contradiction the gaps report names. It is the report's own fix, word for word, and it leaves the "family of configurations" framing that justifies listing every Cairn row. The purpose sentence a few lines later still describes Cairn rows above the best manual row as the reading the table exists to give, with no counterpart for a table where they stand below. The radar still opens with "how much better, and where", so the section would ask "whether" and then assume the answer.

The opening sentence changes to "shows whether Cairn beats …", and the table section's purpose sentence is reworded to match: several Cairn rows standing above the best manual row becomes the reading the table is built to make visible if it holds, and a table where they stand below is published in the same form. The radar section stays as written. The whole ranking-table section then reads as neutral, opener and purpose sentence alike. It keeps the reason every Cairn configuration appears, losers included, and leaves the radar text, which already says it draws whatever the data shows, untouched. The radar's opening line "The radar shows how much better, and where" still assumes a margin exists, so the results section stays neutral in one half and presumptive in the other.

The table's opener and purpose sentence change as in the table-section rewording ("whether", and a losing table published in the same form). The radar's opening line also changes from "how much better, and where" to a neutral form saying whether the Cairn curves sit outside the manual ones, by how much, and on which axes. The rest of the radar text is unchanged, including its no-claim rule and the reasoning behind which curves are drawn. Every sentence that introduces a part of the results section then states a question rather than an answer, which matches the radar's existing "the page states no claim the curves do not" rule and makes the whole page consistent with it. It is the largest of the "whether" edits and reaches into radar prose next to the curve-selection reasoning.
